title: Warn when a few large Git objects consume hundreds of megabytes
description: The Git storage doctor currently reports PASS because 2,850 loose objects are below Git's count-based automatic-cleanup threshold, even though those objects consume 506.3 MiB and the filesystem has only a few hundred MiB free. Large repeated Beads exports make object count a poor safety signal. Detect byte-heavy loose-object growth before it becomes a disk-pressure or iteration-latency problem.
design: Keep diagnosis read-only and make maintenance a separate explicit, backup-first action. Add a reviewed loose-byte threshold and report the largest loose object classes without exposing file contents. Prove any supported packing procedure against a disposable copy and require enough free working space before touching the live object store. Do not put Git metadata deletion inside the general artifact cleanup command.
acceptance_criteria: 1. A fixture proves that low object count plus high loose bytes is a warning or failure, not PASS. 2. The doctor explains count, bytes, automatic Git thresholds, free-space risk, and the safe next command in beginner-friendly language. 3. The source of the large objects is measured without printing sensitive contents. 4. Any maintenance procedure is backup-first, uses supported Git commands, checks available scratch space, and preserves refs, reflogs, stashes, worktrees, index, and exported Beads data. 5. Before and after storage and command latency are recorded. 6. README Goals and North Star impact is recorded.
close_reason: Verified storage repair and durable byte-based recurrence warnings

comments.author: Marcelo Serpa
comments.text:
DIAGNOSTIC SLICE — The read-only doctor previously returned PASS with 2,850 loose Git objects because Git's automatic policy is count-based, even though those objects consumed 506.3 MiB and the filesystem had less free space than that. A type/size-only audit (no object contents printed) found 250 loose blobs at least 7 MiB each accounting for 489.2 MiB on disk. Of those, 123 are definitely reachable versions of .beads/issues.jsonl and consume 243.5 MiB; 126 similarly large blobs are unreachable or no longer named by refs and consume 244.3 MiB; one generated CppTargetCore snapshot consumes 1.4 MiB. This explains why object count was a misleading health signal.

The doctor now adds a project-owned 256 MiB loose-byte review threshold and reports available filesystem space plus conservative maintenance headroom. A synthetic fixture proves two objects reporting 300,000 KiB warn with loose_object_bytes while the Git directory stays byte-identical. The live checkout now warns instead of passing and explicitly says not to run backup or packing while only roughly 348 MiB is free versus 1 GiB of conservative headroom. This slice remains read-only: no Git object was repacked or pruned. Backup-first live maintenance and before/after proof remain required before bead closure. Oracle was deliberately skipped because this is a reproduced, bounded Git-diagnostic seam, not compiler architecture or release semantics. README Goals and North Star bars remain unchanged.

comments.author: Marcelo Serpa
comments.text:
Closure evidence, 2026-07-20.

Practical outcome: Git no longer keeps roughly half a gigabyte of large loose
objects in this checkout, and the read-only storage check will warn before the
same byte-heavy pattern grows this far again.

The measured cause was repeated large file versions, not an unusually high
object count. Before maintenance, Git reported 2,922 loose objects using 513.20
MiB. Of those, 126 reachable versions of `.beads/issues.jsonl` accounted for
261,663,150 bytes on disk. Git's normal automatic-cleanup threshold was 6,700
objects, so both Git and the former project check treated the count as healthy.
The new project-owned 256 MiB byte threshold covers that blind spot, and its
fixture proves that a low count plus high byte use reports a warning without
changing the object store.

Maintenance was backup-first. The retained raw `.git` backup passed
`git fsck --full --no-dangling`. The all-refs bundle is 180,232 KiB, passed
verification, and has SHA-256
`56f9ee2fe1b61ed028c5f6209b9bec5def1667dd5a0488f01a3d93bb9628167f`.
The exact cruft-pack command was rehearsed on a disposable copy before it was
run on the live checkout. The rehearsal initially exposed a test-design error:
the copied Git database names its temporary worktree path, so that location
string cannot be byte-identical to the live path. After normalizing only that
location, the worktree HEAD and branch matched, and every content-bearing state
check was exact.

The live maintenance took 13.40 seconds. `.git` fell from 716,712 KiB to
199,604 KiB; loose objects fell from 2,922 / 513.20 MiB to zero; and the final
store has two packs using about 188.5 MiB. A full post-maintenance `git fsck`
passed. HEAD, refs, all 10,842 reflog entries, reachable and reflog-reachable
objects, index entries, stashes, worktree registration, and the complete Beads
export matched the recorded pre-maintenance values exactly. `git gc --auto` is
now a quiet no-op, `.git/gc.log` is absent, the working tree is clean, and the
live doctor reports PASS.

Twenty warm `git status --short` samples had a 19.74 ms median against the raw
pre-maintenance backup and a 19.82 ms median against the compacted live store.
That is ordinary measurement noise, so this change claims reclaimed disk and a
working early warning, not a status-speed improvement.

The implementation commit is
`f20096441ced9edc9fde9bfcb51942a94ae9785a`. Exact Core run 29796316484 and
Release / Semantic Publish run 29797035786 passed, publishing v0.23.4. The
normal agent and cleanup documentation now requires both read-only storage
doctors before heavy runs and at the end of coding sessions, so recurrence is
not dependent on someone remembering an incident-specific command. Oracle was
deliberately skipped because the work used standard Git backup, integrity, and
packing behavior at a bounded tooling seam. README Goals and North Star bars
remain unchanged because this improves developer-storage safety rather than
compiler production readiness.

title: Keep unreleased high-risk changes pending until exact QA proof
description: Release v0.23.1 was published from Core run 29782777726 because the final report-only commit was correctly classified as Q1 and passed. The candidate also contained immediately preceding runtime and macro-host changes that required Q3, but those older automatic runs were cancelled or superseded and the exact combined Q3 run had not happened yet. Per-push classification therefore allowed a cheap follow-up commit to hide outstanding release risk. Release automation must consider the complete unreleased candidate and its exact proof, not only the final push diff.
design: Keep ordinary per-push routing cheap, but add a fail-closed release-candidate risk/proof contract. Compute cumulative risk from the last accepted release boundary (or another authenticated candidate base) through the candidate commit, require the corresponding exact-head Core evidence, and verify the route/proof receipt before semantic publication. A later cheap commit may preserve or raise the outstanding tier but never lower it. Keep Q3 correctness evidence separate from Q4/Full1 release claims; do not make every 0.x patch run Full1. Treat this as thinking:xhigh release/provenance policy and record a second-pass design review before implementation.
acceptance_criteria: 1. A fixture proves a Q3 implementation followed by Q0/Q1 docs or snapshot commits remains release-blocked until the exact combined head passes Q3. 2. A genuinely Q0/Q1-only unreleased range retains the cheap release path allowed by current 0.x policy. 3. Release automation verifies candidate SHA, cumulative risk tier, Core route receipt, required job results, and run attempt before publishing. 4. Cancelled, skipped, stale, or different-commit evidence fails closed. 5. Q3 does not claim Q4/Full1 readiness, and existing >=1.0 enforcement remains intact. 6. The already-published v0.23.1 event is documented without rewriting tags or pretending prepublication proof existed. 7. Exact pushed workflow tests and a second-pass xhigh review pass. 8. README Goals/North Star impact is recorded.
close_reason: Cumulative unreleased-risk routing and exact Core-run release verification passed locally and in exact pushed workflows; v0.23.2 was published only after the verified Q3 candidate proof.

comments.author: Marcelo Serpa
comments.text:
XHIGH SECOND-PASS DESIGN REVIEW — Oracle is deliberately not requested for this bounded CI/release seam: no compiler semantics, ABI, or product scope is changing, and the failure plus safe ownership boundary are directly evidenced by runs 29782504708, 29782777726, and release 29783154654. A written second pass checked the release/provenance risks before implementation.

Observed behavior: Core classifies only github.event.before..head. When a high-risk run is cancelled by a later cheap push, the cheap head can pass Q1 and trigger semantic-release even though the combined unreleased candidate never passed Q3. v0.23.1 is the concrete incident; it must be documented, not rewritten.

Selected seam: keep PR feedback incremental, but on default-branch pushes compute the risk-driving path inventory from the latest reachable semantic-release tag through the candidate head. Record both the release base tag/SHA and candidate SHA in a versioned route receipt. Therefore a later docs, Beads, or snapshot commit can preserve or raise the unreleased tier but cannot lower it until a new release tag establishes a fresh boundary. If the tag/base cannot be proven, fail safe to Q3.

Release-side defense: the workflow_run release job downloads the exact route artifact from its triggering Core run, verifies repository/workflow/run/attempt/candidate identity, recomputes the tagged-range inventory and policy result from the checked-out candidate, and requires the stable Core aggregate appropriate to that tier before semantic-release. Missing, stale, cancelled, skipped, different-head, or lower-tier evidence stops publication. Existing >=1.0 Full1 RC enforcement remains an additional stronger layer; Q3 is correctness QA, not a Q4 or Full1 claim. Manual provenance dry runs remain non-publishing; any manual publish path must name and verify an exact Core run rather than bypass this proof.

Rejected shortcuts: always run Q3 (wastes the Q0/Q1 gains); trust only the last push diff (the proven bug); infer risk from conventional commit subjects (not a source-surface proof); accept a green workflow label without its route artifact (cannot prove what was required); move or rewrite v0.23.1 (destroys provenance); or require Full1 Q4 for every 0.x patch (changes product policy and cost unnecessarily).

Implementation should be two reviewable slices: first a tested cumulative inventory/receipt that makes the next exact push self-route correctly; second release-side artifact verification and negative fixtures. Stop if release tags are not a reliable authenticated boundary, if the release workflow cannot bind an artifact to the exact run attempt, or if PR routing becomes cumulative and starts re-testing unrelated already-proven main history. README/North Star bars stay unchanged.

comments.author: Marcelo Serpa

title: Fix the 10-second Haxe-host delay in Reflaxe builds
description: The exact Core run 29734148430 spent 1,140 seconds in test:portable, compared with 193 seconds in the accepted sharding baseline run 29686414970. Only three portable fixtures were added, so fixture count alone does not explain the roughly sixfold increase. Find whether the cost comes from the corrected Reflaxe framework, repeated Haxe startup and typing, native builds, lost caches, runner contention, or another bounded cause, then shorten the suite without deleting behavior coverage.
design: Add output-inert timing around each fixture's Haxe generation, Dune build, executable check, and any repeated lowering-report build. Compare the same commit locally and on a clean hosted runner. Optimize only after the dominant repeated work is measured. Safe candidates include reusing immutable exact-revision compiler inputs, preserving target build caches, or bounded parallel fixture execution; any server or cache reuse must honor the revision and lifecycle contracts from haxe_ocaml-7201t.
acceptance_criteria: 1. Exact per-phase evidence explains the 193s to 1140s change or classifies it as reproducible host contention. 2. The portable suite retains every fixture and behavior assertion. 3. Any parallelism or reuse is deterministic, revision-safe, and does not share mutable output directories. 4. Focused local runs and an exact pushed Core run demonstrate a material latency improvement without increasing flakes or weakening the Tests aggregate. 5. The measured before/after runner time and README/North Star impact are recorded.
close_reason: The measured lifecycle hashing regression is fixed, the full 75-fixture suite remains intact, exact Core and cross-host package workflows pass, and hosted target-package time fell 72.5% without weakening required checks.

comments.author: Marcelo Serpa
comments.text: ROOT-SYMPTOM EVIDENCE — The same exact installed-package method isolates the regression outside native OCaml work. Linux run 29705893746 at f9b6f879d measured warm full-Haxe/target/outside-target medians of 1,173/73/1,100 ms and one-file medians of 1,467/350/1,118 ms. After the corrected Reflaxe lifecycle pin, run 29734148492 at a3afbcd7c measured 11,159/70/11,091 ms warm and 11,390/308/11,084 ms for one file. Dune and target-owned work stayed equal or improved, while startup/typing/generation/orchestration outside those subprocesses grew about tenfold. The Core portable suite shows the same pattern: 193.064s became 1,140.147s with only three added fixtures. Treat these as one P0 developer-loop regression. First compare the host/framework phases between the two exact revisions; do not optimize Dune or delete fixtures because neither explains the data.

comments.author: Marcelo Serpa
comments.text: Root cause confirmed: the Reflaxe lifecycle rendered and SHA-256-hashed every complete typed function body around every expression-cleanup pass. A small compiler-sized fixture performed 4,569 full-body digests and took about 7.4 seconds warm even when no target files changed. The shared, target-neutral fix landed in fullofcaffeine/reflaxe PR #10 (merge 62260d866f31951dfd428f1df45ea127ea9dbcf8): structural marker families now compare their marker inventory per pass and hash the complete body only at lifecycle entry/exit; exact-body families and trace mode remain strict per pass. Six fork CI checks passed. With the pinned merge commit, the same fixture performs 1,065 digests and warm wall samples are 2.65s, 2.51s, and 2.83s with identical generated output. Upstream main was rechecked at 73a983112e039daad46b37912ab238df6bf0cf53 before advancing the fork pin. Broad portable/package/Core evidence is still pending. README Goals and North Star bars remain unchanged because this is an internal iteration-speed repair, not new user-facing compiler coverage.

comments.author: Marcelo Serpa
comments.text: Second bounded optimization: reflaxe.ocaml now captures one exact function/body binding for the read-only place-planning walk, reuses it for every operation and inventory record, and relies on the lifecycle exit observation plus a fresh emission-time observation to reject later mutation. The focused lifecycle suite, feature-gated/standalone portable fixtures, deterministic trace check, and late-body-mutation negative all pass. Digest calls on the compiler probe fell again from 1,065 to 764; warm wall samples are 2.18s, 2.08s, and 2.23s. Generated output remains unchanged. The unchanged full portable suite passed in 373.08s after only the framework fix (down from 1,140.15s, but still above the earlier 193.06s baseline); remeasurement after this target batching and bounded fixture parallelism remains pending. README/North Star bars remain unchanged.

comments.author: Marcelo Serpa
comments.text: Bounded fixture scheduling restores the broad gate without dropping coverage. scripts/test-portable.sh now defaults to two independent workers; every worker starts a separate Haxe process and owns one fixture out/ directory, while the parent buffers and replays detailed logs in sorted fixture order. PORTABLE_JOBS=1 retains the serial diagnostic route and PORTABLE_FIXTURE_ALLOWLIST remains supported. Unit tests prove bounded concurrency and input-order results; a forced Haxe-worker failure propagates and names both failed fixtures. The exact 75-fixture suite passed in 187.85s (user 387.94s, sys 185.84s), compared with 373.08s serial after the framework fix, 1,140.15s at the regression commit, and the accepted 193.06s pre-regression baseline. No fixture or assertion was removed. FAST_LOCAL_VALIDATION.md documents the controls. README Goals/North Star bars remain unchanged because the result restores development throughput rather than adding product capability.

comments.author: Marcelo Serpa
comments.text: Local broad and release-shaped evidence is green on implementation commit 5b6d8a166d2a0bee8c75d5b68cf9221ac947876c with a clean worktree. Target-packages timings: test:portable 187.85s, test:snapshot 26.53s, test:examples 124.72s, total 339.10s. This is slightly faster than the accepted pre-regression total of 342.28s (193.06 + 16.55 + 132.66) and 77% faster than the regressed 1,467.95s total. The release-shaped package install passed in 24.52s with archive SHA 596e74d5b0616923a8ce7e8ddd2be5a09356ad38d87c3bd56bba7c82dafd3448, Reflaxe merge 62260d866f31951dfd428f1df45ea127ea9dbcf8, exact content SHA 8aae1f171fd5a17413ba3ead685db779d1fa05670eb86d8eab44633b0cc34c48, reproducible package=true, and matching runtime output. Exact pushed Core and package-matrix evidence remains before closure. README/North Star bars remain unchanged.

comments.author: Marcelo Serpa
comments.text:
CLOSURE EVIDENCE — The 10-second host-side regression is removed without deleting test coverage. Exact pushed commit dc4d4c370ccce69eacd9e8e7e437a3ae20af5aad passed Core PR Checks run 29739793804 and source-package matrix run 29739793842. In the Core target-packages job 88344580139, all 75 portable fixtures and their existing assertions passed in 227.162s; snapshots passed in 36.632s; examples passed in 139.371s; total 403.167s. The regressed exact run took 1,467.950s, so the hosted total fell by 72.5%. The earlier accepted hosted total was 342.277s; the current exact local total was 339.10s, so the remaining hosted difference is runner/setup variation rather than the sixfold compiler regression. The pool is capped at two isolated workers, preserves a one-worker diagnostic mode, uses separate Haxe processes and output directories, replays detailed logs deterministically, and propagates worker failures. No fixture, assertion, or required Tests aggregate dependency was removed.

The package matrix independently installed one reproducible source archive on macOS arm64 and Linux x64 and passed runtime, provenance, performance-receipt, and cross-host consistency checks. Archive SHA-256 was 596e74d5b0616923a8ce7e8ddd2be5a09356ad38d87c3bd56bba7c82dafd3448; Reflaxe fork commit 62260d866f31951dfd428f1df45ea127ea9dbcf8 and content digest 8aae1f171fd5a17413ba3ead685db779d1fa05670eb86d8eab44633b0cc34c48 were recorded. Linux warm full-Haxe / target-owned / remaining-host medians improved from 11,159 / 70 / 11,091 ms in the regression to 3,494 / 91 / 3,403 ms; one-file medians improved from 11,390 / 308 / 11,084 ms to 3,810 / 382 / 3,428 ms. macOS independently passed at 3,527 / 211 / 3,289 ms warm and 4,006 / 825 / 3,187 ms for one file; absolute cross-host ranking remains forbidden.

The cause and fix are bounded: full typed function bodies had been rendered and hashed around every cleanup step. The target-neutral fork fix keeps full-body checks at lifecycle boundaries for marker-only tracking, while exact-body tracking and trace mode retain strict checks; reflaxe.ocaml also reuses one already-validated body binding during each read-only planning walk. README Goals and North Star bars remain unchanged because this restores internal development speed without adding compiler capability. Further absolute latency improvements remain report-only work under parent haxe_ocaml-850ii and the Full1 performance owner; this bead closes only the measured ten-second regression and broad-gate slowdown.

title: Design the Haxe-authored native compiler-transform SDK and Coro proof
description:
Let Haxe developers author native compiler plugins in Haxe, compile them through reflaxe.ocaml, and load the resulting semantic payload from stock Haxe 4.3.7 and hxhx. This bead owns the pre-backend compiler-transform profile: lifecycle hooks, compiler snapshots, validated rewrites, diagnostics, and compiler-server safety. It complements, but does not absorb, M22's post-typing backend and target SDK.

The first cross-host example should be deliberately small and beginner-readable: a Haxe-authored equivalent of the official Haxe native-plugin example that exposes a callable function, reports a source position, and performs one bounded after-typing body rewrite. Coro in ../Coro is the advanced workload because it rewrites typed functions into resumable state machines. Coro is an end-state proof, not the first ABI fixture.
design:
Use two separately versioned semantic profiles over a shared native artifact and developer-tooling substrate: compiler-transform/v1 for Stage4 lifecycle and typed-tree work, and backend-target/v1 for M22 emission. Never expose private upstream Haxe or hxhx OCaml values, mutable compiler globals, or host object identity across the shared ABI. Prefer immutable, stable-ID snapshots plus validated coarse rewrite operations, with exact lifecycle and program-revision rules.

Attempt one identical payload on the supported OCaml/Haxe toolchain. Permit thin host loader shells only after a measured compiler/runtime/linker/loader incompatibility; shells contain no plugin semantics. Stock Haxe activation must use the real Haxe 4.3.7 plugin/macro lifecycle and must not be described as dynamic target registration.

Treat a Haxe port of Coro as provenance-sensitive work. Freeze behavior fixtures and licensing/attribution first. A derived port may reuse Coro under its MIT license with the required notice and a provenance ledger, but it must not mechanically translate private upstream Haxe compiler source. Ask for an independent architecture review before implementation because typed-tree identity, rewrite validation, phase ordering, and server reuse are thinking:xhigh decisions.
acceptance_criteria: 1) A reviewed architecture contract distinguishes compiler-transform/v1 from backend-target/v1 and assigns lifecycle ownership to Stage4/customization. 2) The contract defines shared payload identity, ABI/version negotiation, loader-shell fallback, cache keys, trust, and packaging for stock Haxe and hxhx. 3) A staged example plan starts with an official-example-equivalent Haxe plugin and progresses through a bounded Coro subset to a behavior-compatible Coro-class proof. 4) Typed snapshots, stable identities, validated patches, phase ordering, diagnostics, invalidation, and compiler-server reset semantics have explicit invariants. 5) The developer workflow covers init, watch, build, inspect generated OCaml, test on both hosts, package, install, doctor, publish, and direct-OCaml escape hatches. 6) Generated OCaml quality has enforceable idiom, warning, formatting, runtime-use, size, allocation, and direct-OCaml comparison evidence. 7) Existing M22 and customization beads are linked without readiness inflation. 8) GPT-5.6 Pro or an equivalent written xhigh second pass reviews the plan before implementation.
notes: Native-power checkpoint integration 2026-07-18: Coro-class compiler transforms stay upstream of the OCaml target-lowering boundary. They may emit ordinary normalized Haxe control or transform-owned state machines, but they do not justify a target-wide CFG. Haxe-authored transform/plugin examples should consume the shared authoring and packaging workflow under haxe_ocaml-1hd2w and M22.11 while retaining typed OCaml adapters as an explicit lower-level escape hatch.

comments.author: Marcelo Serpa
comments.text:
ARCHITECTURE CHECKPOINT — 2026-07-18

Current evidence: stock Haxe 4.3.7 exposes native eval-VM plugin loading and after-typing hooks, but no stable dynamic target-registration API. The official example performs a typed field-body rewrite. ../Coro is MIT-licensed and is a substantially stronger after-typing workload: its native OCaml plugin rewrites typed closures into state machines and must preserve control flow, captures, exceptions, and evaluation order.

Planning decision: use two separately versioned semantic profiles over one shared artifact/tooling substrate. compiler-transform/v1 belongs to Stage4/customization and uses candidate-bound typed snapshots plus validated program-revision patches. backend-target/v1 remains M22-owned after the backend-facing program is frozen. They may share payload identity, ABI negotiation, loaders, caches, packaging, testing, trust, and shipping tools, but never a mutable compiler context or one ambiguous semantic API.

Example sequence: first a beginner-readable Haxe-authored equivalent of the official plugin (greeting, position, one bounded body rewrite) loaded by stock Haxe and hxhx; separately, one real promoted Reflaxe target under M22; then one bounded Coro suspension; finally a Coro-class transform. The Coro port must preserve MIT notice/provenance and cannot import upstream Haxe compiler source or tests.

Docs: HAXE_AUTHORED_NATIVE_PLUGIN_TARGET_SDK_PLAN.md is the review candidate. GPT_5_6_PRO_HAXE_NATIVE_PLUGIN_TARGET_SDK_REVIEW_PROMPT.md requests an independent xhigh review before implementation. README/North Star bars remain unchanged because this slice adds planning only.

The existing review package already asks for workflow, escape-hatch, generated-code, and direct-OCaml evidence, so this is a supplemental priority statement rather than an archive-integrity change. It adds no current support or README readiness.

title: Stop Haxe server leaks and clean stale compiler servers
description: Local development accumulated more than 500 Haxe --wait server processes. That makes diagnostics noisy, wastes process-table and memory resources, and can hide real build contention. Inventory the servers safely, remove stale listeners now, and repair the repo-owned server lifecycle so commands reuse or stop their own servers instead of leaking one per run.
design: Prefer one reusable repo-owned server with an explicit identity/ownership record, or no server when reuse cannot be proven. Cleanup must validate process command and ownership before signaling. Global cleanup remains an explicit user-authorized operation; ordinary commands may only reap their own repo server. Keep unrelated active compiler processes out of scope.
acceptance_criteria: 1) Record the pre-cleanup count, ownership/age/port evidence, and distinguish Haxe servers from active compiler jobs. 2) Terminate the user-authorized stale Haxe --wait servers without killing unrelated non-server compiler work. 3) Identify and fix the repo-owned lifecycle path that can leak servers, including success, failure, timeout, and signal cleanup. 4) Add deterministic fixture coverage proving repeated runs do not increase live server count and cleanup is scoped. 5) Make heavy profiling run the existing capacity preflight before spending minutes under invalid host load. 6) Document the fast normal workflow and explicit global cleanup escape hatch. 7) Run shell/Node checks, lifecycle fixtures, relevant guards, and exact pushed CI. 8) Record README Goals/North Star and plugin ABI status.
notes:
thinking:medium initially: bounded process lifecycle and runner plumbing. Escalate to thinking:high only if fixing it changes compiler or plugin architecture.
2026-07-18 evidence: inventory found 533 orphaned native Haxe --wait children plus two live launcher/native pairs (535 server processes total), about 654.6 MiB aggregate RSS; 514 native orphans had /Users/fullofcaffeine/workspace/code/haxe.elixir.codex as cwd. Two unrelated /tmp/haxe-c-import-* compiler experiments were active one-shot work and were deliberately excluded. title: Extract known C++ signature tables to shorten hxhx rebuilds
description: Fresh hxhx builds still spend most of their generation time in the oversized C++ backend module. Move the existing standard-library method argument and return carrier tables into one documented C++ target module so Reflaxe compiles a smaller CppTargetCore without changing how calls are selected or emitted. This is a mechanical ownership and build-latency slice, not a new type system, runtime behavior, or plugin ABI.
design: Use a small service record only for existing scope-aware type rendering and class lookup callbacks. The extracted module may classify already-known stdlib owner/method names, but it must not inspect source bodies, rebind Haxe semantics, add runtime stubs, or change carrier rules. Generated output should remain byte-for-byte identical for representative focused inputs.
acceptance_criteria: 1) Capture a comparable pre-change per-class generation baseline. 2) Move the existing known standard-library method argument/return and prelude signature tables into a documented target-owned module with no duplicated policy left behind. 3) Preserve generated C++ and runtime behavior with focused source-shape and executable coverage. 4) Record before/after CppTargetCore line count, per-module generation time, combined generation time/size, and full build wall time. 5) Run formatter, focused C++ tests, architecture/mega-file guards, current-source/bootstrap verification, and exact pushed CI. 6) Record that README Goals/North Star and the shared stock-Haxe/hxhx plugin ABI are unchanged unless user-visible readiness actually changes.
notes:
thinking:high: this affects a compiler target ownership seam and requires a written second-pass review before closure. GPT/Oracle escalation is not expected unless the extraction exposes unclear semantic ownership.
Implementation checkpoint (2026-07-18): moved the existing known stdlib method argument/return carrier tables into documented CppKnownStdlibSignatures behind a cached service boundary. CppTargetCore fell from 25,753 to 25,251 lines. Focused render and full generated/native C++ smoke passed; incremental bootstrap regeneration plus Dune verification passed. Initial adjacent samples were 208s/87,879ms core before and 196s/84,584ms core + 135ms extracted module after, but an identical after repeat took 221s/98,123ms core. These are not closure-grade speed evidence: the existing capacity checker reported sustained load 2.298 per CPU on a 12-core host (limit 1.5), with unrelated long-running haxe.c compiler experiments consuming CPU. Peak RSS also ranged 1,564-2,493MB, confirming unstable sampling. Keep this bead open until a capacity-passing repeat exists. README Goals/North Star progress bars unchanged; the shared stock-Haxe/hxhx native Reflaxe ABI and loader-shell policy are unchanged. GPT/Oracle escalation remains deliberately skipped because this is a mechanical relocation of an already-tested target table, not a semantic redesign.

title: Make local Beads commands fast without risking issue history
description: Routine issue-tracker operations are now a visible development bottleneck: recent comment, close, and create commands took roughly 27 to more than 90 seconds, while .beads uses about 750 MiB across the embedded Dolt store, retained backup data, and daemon logs. The hook fast path removed redundant imports, but direct Beads commands still delay every checkpoint. Profile and reduce this cost without losing issue records, comments, dependency history, or the tracked JSONL export.
design: Measure command phases, database tables and history, daemon health, Dolt storage, log rotation, backup retention, and export/import cost separately. Take and verify a restorable backup before compaction or retention changes. Use supported Beads and Dolt maintenance commands rather than deleting database files. Keep the tracked .beads/issues.jsonl contract intact and distinguish local transient storage from repository history. Add a documented, repeatable maintenance path and guard against silent data loss or stale export state.
acceptance_criteria: 1) Retained baselines cover read and write commands, export/import, database and log sizes, daemon state, Beads/Dolt versions, and issue/comment/dependency counts. 2) A verified rollback artifact exists before any compaction or retention action. 3) Supported maintenance materially improves routine command latency and storage, or evidence identifies the upstream blocker. 4) Issue, comment, label, dependency, status, and tracked JSONL counts/content remain consistent. 5) Hook synchronization and a two-repository real-change control remain green. 6) Log and backup retention are explicit and conservative. 7) Recovery and regular maintenance commands are documented for contributors. 8) Full repository guards, pull/export/push, and README Goals/North Star review are recorded.
close_reason: Verified empty legacy database removed through supported Dolt lifecycle after restore-tested backups; read/write latency and memory materially improved, a read-only doctor and safe recovery docs landed, full local guards and exact pushed Core CI Guardrails pass.

comments.author: Marcelo Serpa
comments.text:
Measured root cause and safe maintenance checkpoint. The active Beads 1.0.4 store contained the current haxe_ocaml database plus a legacy database named beads. The legacy database exported zero issues, but adding it beside a compact active database changed bd show from 1.03s to 21.62s and bd ready from 0.81s to 35.69s. This proved that embedded Dolt was opening the unused sibling database on every command.

Before maintenance, the checkout held 1,910 issues, 2,828 comments, 2,018 dependencies, and 7,178 labels. The canonical full export SHA-256 was 614ce1d2027f1ad8aebb3f11623251ae26d248db5b5d2de356968299ae1cdada. A Beads-native full-history backup was restored into an isolated repository, then re-exported byte-for-byte with the same SHA. The backup archive SHA-256 is 16e7c34b19778b6fb267f2a906b303bf75f9ff53a52e4134267c5014d5877e4c. A second raw snapshot was also verified before mutation.

The maintenance used Dolt 1.86.4, the exact version embedded by Beads 1.0.4. In an isolated copy first, DROP DATABASE beads removed only the zero-issue legacy database, and the official dolt_purge_dropped_databases procedure reclaimed its tombstoned files. The same sequence was then applied to the checkout. The active export remained byte-identical. Total local .beads storage fell from about 926 MiB to 217 MiB; the active embedded store is now 67 MiB instead of roughly 775 MiB across two databases.

Post-maintenance timings: bd show is 1.44s and 161,267,712 bytes maximum RSS versus 26.25s and 2,739,748,864 bytes before; bd ready is 0.95s and 159,285,248 bytes versus 37.21s and 3,119,611,904 bytes; full export is 1.48s versus 23.53s. This is roughly 18x, 39x, and 16x faster respectively, with about 17x to 20x lower peak memory on the measured reads.

Beads 1.1.0 was tested separately. It is stable, but its schema migration intentionally rekeys comment IDs and updates many issue timestamps, causing broad tracked JSONL churn. That upgrade is deliberately deferred to a dedicated migration review rather than mixed into this storage repair. README Goals and North Star bars remain unchanged because this improves contributor workflow without changing compiler production readiness.

title: Restore safe, fast Git maintenance for the development checkout
description: The main checkout currently holds roughly 15,404 loose Git objects using about 1.39 GiB, and .git/gc.log reports that automatic cleanup stopped because too many unreachable objects accumulated. This can slow ordinary Git operations and keeps avoidable disk pressure in the main compiler development loop. Diagnose and repair the repository safely without risking reachable work, reflogs, user changes, or Beads history.
design: Measure object counts, pack state, reflog protection, worktrees, stashes, and the exact reason automatic maintenance is disabled before changing anything. Take a verifiable metadata/object backup or equivalent rollback point. Prefer supported git maintenance, repack, and prune-expiry controls with a conservative grace period; never run a blind immediate git prune. Measure no-op status, fetch/pull, object counts, and disk usage before and after. Keep the separate .beads database/log/backup footprint outside Git object cleanup and file another bounded bead if its own retention policy needs work.
acceptance_criteria: 1) Before evidence records Git version, object/pack counts, disk usage, gc.log, reflogs, stashes, worktrees, and representative command latency. 2) A verified rollback path exists before any object deletion or repack. 3) Maintenance preserves reachable branches, tags, reflogs, stashes, worktrees, and the exact working tree. 4) Object storage and relevant command latency materially improve or the bead records why cleanup is unsafe. 5) Automatic maintenance is restored with documented conservative settings and a repeatable command. 6) Beads storage is measured separately and not deleted as part of Git cleanup. 7) Repository guards, status, pull, export, and push remain healthy. 8) README Goals and North Star bars are reviewed and recorded unchanged unless production readiness changes.
close_reason: Verified raw backup and bundle, trialed supported cruft-pack maintenance, reduced .git from 1.7 GiB to 196 MiB while preserving refs/reflogs/reachable state and Beads data, restored automatic maintenance, documented recovery, and passed full local plus exact pushed Guardrails.

comments.author: Marcelo Serpa
comments.text:
Measured repair and thinking-high second-pass review (2026-07-18). Git 2.40.1 began from a clean synchronized main checkout with one worktree, no stashes, 78 branch/remote/tag refs, 10,190 reflog entries, and 51,478 reachable objects. It held 15,462 loose objects using 1.41 GiB, 38 packs using 265.72 MiB, and 1.7 GiB total .git storage. A full scan found 15,713 objects unreachable even when reflogs were included. gc.log contained the automatic-maintenance failure saying there were too many unreachable loose objects. Baseline git status was 0.05s, no-op pull was 0.76s, and the separate .beads store was 218 MiB. The complete 1,911-record Beads export SHA-256 was 3b083abaa541682fde45666454675bbd715c333d0924be3350bbb603c4ceda49.

Rollback was established before mutation. A raw copy-on-write Git-directory snapshot preserved refs, reflogs, index, config, and unreachable objects; its full fsck passed with no output. An independent all-refs bundle verified successfully and has SHA-256 d152cce62e91229d4db0eb5b50986118f168be07ef0ee463d26513e74a782e35. Semantic ref, reflog, and reachable-object inventories matched the checkout exactly. Dry runs showed that direct pruning with the standard two-week grace would remove only 319 objects (20.7 MiB), while immediate pruning could remove roughly 1.39 GiB; immediate pruning was rejected.

The selected boundary is Git cruft packs with the standard two-week prune grace. The exact GC command preserved every reflog entry for the one-time run and was trialed on a disposable clone of the raw backup first. That trial reduced 1.7 GiB to 188 MiB, loose objects from 15,468 to zero, and packs from 38 to two while retaining a cruft-pack .mtimes sidecar. Refs, all 10,190 reflog entries, reachable objects, and a full fsck remained identical/green.

The same supported command was then applied to the clean main checkout with no concurrent Git writer, after setting local gc.cruftPacks=true. Main .git storage is now 196 MiB, with zero loose objects and two packs using 183.83 MiB. HEAD, 78 refs, 10,190 reflog entries, 51,478 reachable objects, index hash, worktree inventory, empty stash inventory, clean status, and the byte-identical Beads export all survived. Full fsck passed with no output in 89.93s; git gc --auto is a 0.00s quiet no-op; gc.log is absent; status is 0.07s and no-op pull is 0.61s. The timing differences are treated as noise: the proven gain is about 1.5 GiB reclaimed plus restored automatic-maintenance health.

Second-pass safety result: no git prune --expire=now, no git gc --aggressive, no deletion below .git/objects, and no reflog expiry were used. Both rollback artifacts remain retained through push verification. The checked-in doctor invokes only Git version, rev-parse, count-objects, and read-only config getters plus filesystem reads. Fixtures fingerprint the whole temporary Git directory before/after healthy and warning cases, prove gc.log and loose objects are not changed, cover SKIP/PASS/WARN, and fail closed on malformed counts. The backup-first guide requires a clean checkout, no concurrent writer, raw backup plus bundle, isolated trial, semantic comparisons, and fsck. Focused fixtures, the current doctor, real two-repository post-checkout control, local-path guard, and the complete npm run ci:guards suite pass. README Goals and North Star bars remain unchanged because this repairs contributor storage/maintenance rather than compiler production readiness.

title: Make no-op Git checkouts fast without skipping Beads sync
description: An ordinary git pull --rebase with no remote changes spent about two minutes after fetch. The attached process tree showed Git rebasing a commit onto the identical commit and invoking bd hooks run post-checkout with the same old and new SHA. The installed Beads 1.0.4 hook eventually succeeded, but this turns a no-op pull into a major contributor delay. Remove that avoidable work while preserving real issue import/export and all safety hooks.
design: Profile the identical-SHA post-checkout path and compare it with a real changed-tree checkout. Prefer a repository-owned, fixture-tested fast guard at the narrowest safe hook boundary: a branch checkout with identical old/new object IDs cannot have changed tracked checkout content, so it should not pay for a full Beads import scan. Real SHA changes, file checkouts, ambiguous arguments, and explicit Beads commands must continue through the canonical bd hooks run path. Use the supported hook installer/chaining model, keep user hook content safe, and do not disable automatic tracker synchronization globally. Measure Git loose-object maintenance separately so hook and repository-storage costs are not conflated.
acceptance_criteria: 1) Retained before evidence records the exact command, old/new SHA, hook child process, Beads version, issue-export size, loose-object state, and wall time. 2) The repository hook integration exits quickly only for the proven identical-commit branch-checkout shape; changed SHAs, file-checkout flags, missing/malformed arguments, and manual Beads operations still use canonical synchronization. 3) Installer behavior is idempotent, preserves/chains existing user and Beads hooks, and has focused fixtures for install, reinstall, fast path, and real-change delegation. 4) A real temporary-repository control proves issue JSONL changes still import/export after checkout. 5) Before/after samples show a material no-op pull or direct-hook latency reduction without slowing the real-change path. 6) Documentation explains the optimization and a deterministic recovery/reinstall command. 7) Focused hooks, tracker, local-path, shell, and broad repository guards pass. 8) README Goals and North Star bars remain unchanged unless user-facing production readiness changes.
close_reason: Closed

comments.author: Marcelo Serpa
comments.text:
Implementation checkpoint before the first code commit.

Measured cause: an attached no-op git pull --rebase invoked bd hooks run post-checkout with identical old/new commit 353febcdcfc4279ca8f0665a3c087e23e9d3c28f and branch flag 1, then waited about two minutes. A direct timed canonical hook reproduction took 122.95 seconds (153.45s user, 12.86s system) and reached 2,001,895,424 bytes maximum resident memory. Its active child was bd import --quiet .beads/issues.jsonl. The export held 1,907 issues and 7,481,949 bytes. That import also replaced a newer local in-progress claim with the older staged open record, so the redundant work was a correctness hazard as well as latency. Git separately had 15,404 loose objects using 1.39 GiB; that storage issue is deliberately not conflated with or changed by this hook slice.

Implemented boundary: npm run hooks:install now preserves the official Beads shim as the real-change delegate and installs a repository-owned post-checkout guard. The guard skips Beads only when Git supplies exactly three valid arguments, the branch flag is 1, old and new object IDs match the actual current HEAD, and the recorded last successfully synchronized branch-or-detached identity plus HEAD also matches. A different branch at the same commit, a changed commit, file checkout, missing or malformed arguments, stale state, and a prior failed Beads delegate all take the canonical path. Existing custom user hooks are preserved and run first. Successful delegation records state atomically; failed delegation leaves state stale so the next event retries. Reinstallation is idempotent and conflicting custom hooks fail closed.

Final identical-branch-and-commit samples were 0.06s, 0.07s, and 0.06s, for a 0.06s median versus the 122.95s canonical reproduction (about 2,049 times faster). The fake-hook fixture proves install/reinstall, official delegate preservation, user-hook chaining, exact-argument delegation, equal-commit branch-switch delegation, file/malformed handling, SHA/HEAD validation, failed-delegate retry, and custom-hook conflict refusal. The opt-in real-bd smoke created two temporary repositories and proved a changed checkout imported an issue that existed only in the target branch.

Second-pass design review required by thinking:high was performed explicitly. It caught two unsafe early assumptions before commit: equal object IDs alone do not distinguish a same-commit branch switch, and branch-only state could hide a prior failed import after HEAD changed. The final branch-plus-HEAD state and delegate-success rule address both, with focused coverage. Oracle was not escalated because the seam remained bounded and the failure mechanism was directly measured.

Validation: npm run test:hooks:post-checkout passes; npm run test:hooks:post-checkout:real passes with real Beads 1.0.4; shell and Node syntax checks pass; local-path and diff checks pass; and the complete npm run ci:guards bundle passes on the final design, including the official formatter over 718 Haxe files (88.361s total). Beginner testing and fast-validation docs explain installation, recovery, semantics, measurements, and limitations. README Goals and North Star bars remain unchanged because this shortens contributor workflow without changing production readiness. A real post-commit no-op pull and exact pushed CI remain required before closure.

On the exact final commit, /usr/bin/time -lp env HXHX_HOOK_TRACE=1 git pull --rebase completed in 0.74s with 12,320,768 bytes maximum resident memory and printed the guarded skip marker; no bd import ran. That is about 274 times faster than the 202.75s end-to-end lifecycle control. The earlier direct canonical import baseline remains 122.95s and 2,001,895,424 bytes.

Exact implementation commits e6d6fd66 and c9bd637c were pushed to main. GitHub Actions Core PR Checks run 29645231070 passed Guardrails job 88082280246 in 3m22s on c9bd637c. The separate Git storage finding (about 15,404 loose objects / 1.39 GiB and disabled automatic maintenance) is not changed here and will receive its own measured, backup-aware bead. The GitHub Actions Node runtime deprecation warning is likewise separate workflow maintenance.

title: Measure installed reflaxe.ocaml performance on Linux and macOS
description: The current target-performance baseline is a local darwin-arm64 snapshot from 2026-03-13. It does not prove current package performance on the two verified package hosts and cannot support platform-wide expectations. Measure one exact installed source ZIP on clean Ubuntu and macOS runners, retain raw samples and host metadata, and report each platform independently.
design: Use one clean package producer and give its exact ZIP and manifest to Linux and macOS performance consumers. Extend or wrap the deterministic reflaxe.ocaml performance runner so scenarios resolve the installed target from a disposable haxelib repository instead of the checkout. Preserve the existing six-scenario method: clean emitted output per build repetition, native build timing, emitted ML and executable size, verified hot-loop output, and portable-versus-metal ratios. Retain raw samples, CPU/OS/toolchain/load facts, package and manifest identities, and an artifact-opened aggregate. Treat this as report and freshness evidence, not a cross-host absolute threshold or broad support claim; keep the existing reference baseline until enough repeated evidence justifies a reviewed replacement.
acceptance_criteria: 1) One clean producer builds the deterministic reflaxe.ocaml ZIP and publishes its exact commit, version, manifest, and SHA. 2) Ubuntu and macOS jobs install and benchmark that exact ZIP with stock Haxe 4.3.7 and a pinned OCaml/Dune toolchain, without resolving reflaxe.ocaml from the checkout. 3) All six canonical scenarios retain raw build samples, runtime samples where applicable, output verification, emitted ML bytes/count, executable bytes, and portable-versus-metal ratios. 4) Each receipt records platform, architecture, CPU count/model when available, runner image, toolchain versions, load/capacity context, command/method version, package SHA, and clean provenance without machine-local paths. 5) An aggregate opens the producer and both receipts, rejects mixed or stale evidence, and emits a stable per-platform performance marker without asserting that Linux and macOS timings should match. 6) Negative fixtures cover wrong package/commit/host, missing raw samples, unverified output, malformed metrics, and accidental checkout resolution. 7) Public performance docs explain freshness, per-host results, method, limitations, and the difference from hxhx compiler/plugin performance. 8) Full local guards and one exact pushed workflow pass; README Goals and North Star bars change only if the evidence materially changes user-facing readiness.
close_reason: Exact installed-package Linux/macOS performance matrix is implemented, documented, locally guarded, and green on pushed workflow run 29643502308 with retained same-package receipts and aggregate proof.

title: Prove one reflaxe.ocaml ZIP on Linux and macOS
description: A package rebuilt independently on each runner can hide host-dependent archive differences and does not prove that users receive the artifact CI tested. Build one release-shaped reflaxe.ocaml source ZIP, pass that exact artifact to clean Linux and macOS install jobs, and retain comparable evidence for both hosts.
design: Add a dedicated package-evidence workflow with one designated archive builder and a two-host validation matrix. Extend the isolated-install runner with a supplied-ZIP mode that validates the filename, metadata version, source-only contents, and SHA without rebuilding it. Each platform installs the downloaded ZIP into a disposable haxelib repository and runs the same external application. Keep this source haxelib artifact independent of future native plugin payload/loader packaging. Describe Linux and macOS as verified hosts only; do not make a broad support or Windows claim in this bead.
acceptance_criteria: 1) One CI job builds the canonical deterministic source ZIP once and publishes its commit, version, file count, size, SHA-256, and source-only result. 2) Ubuntu and macOS jobs download and validate that exact ZIP without rebuilding it. 3) Both jobs use stock Haxe 4.3.7, install into disposable haxelib repositories, compile/build/run the external app, and match expected output. 4) Per-host summaries retain sanitized toolchain, timing, installed-path, emitted-source, executable, and stdout identities tied to the shared ZIP SHA. 5) A focused fixture rejects a supplied ZIP with the wrong name/version/hash or forbidden contents. 6) CI uploads builder and per-host evidence with stable markers, and a guard protects the one-builder/many-consumers contract. 7) Documentation clearly separates verified hosts from declared product support and from future native-plugin loader packaging. 8) README Goals and North Star bars remain unchanged unless this evidence materially changes user-facing readiness.
close_reason: One deterministic reflaxe.ocaml 0.18.19 source ZIP now has exact clean-commit producer evidence, successful isolated stock-Haxe/native execution on Ubuntu and macOS, an artifact-opened aggregate receipt, focused negative fixtures, full local guards, sanitized retained evidence, and honest support boundaries.

title: Prove the reflaxe.ocaml zip in an isolated external app

acceptance_criteria: 1) The canonical release script builds a reflaxe.ocaml zip whose version matches repository metadata. 2) The zip installs into a disposable haxelib repository without reading reflaxe.ocaml from the checkout. 3) An original nontrivial external app compiles with upstream Haxe 4.3.7, builds through Dune, runs, and matches checked-in expected output. 4) Evidence records commit, zip SHA-256, Haxe/OCaml/Dune versions, installed target path, emitted artifact identity, and runtime result without machine-local path leakage. 5) Focused negative coverage rejects missing or checkout-resolved target packages. 6) The smoke is available through a stable command and appropriate CI path. 7) README Goals and North Star bars remain unchanged until cross-platform package evidence and the broader parent acceptance criteria pass.

title: Add a safe fast current-source hxhx profile
description: A measured Stage0 build with Reflaxe expression preprocessors disabled emitted the same focused C++ output, passed OCaml/JS, native plugin, and macro-host smoke checks, and reduced comparable emit time from 211 seconds to 150 seconds. Developers need an explicit reusable command for this faster compiler without allowing it into exact parity, release, or current-source proof lanes.
design: Add a separately named no-prepass-dev build/selector with its own output directory and provenance metadata. Record the build profile in every current-source receipt. Strict and ordinary developer validators require the full profile; the fast validator requires no-prepass-dev. Keep Gate 2, Gate 3, release, and exact current-source commands unchanged. The fast artifact may be used only for focused iteration, and unsupported or divergent behavior must be rechecked with the full compiler.
acceptance_criteria: 1) A documented npm command builds and reuses the no-prepass developer compiler in an isolated output directory. 2) Metadata records full versus no-prepass-dev, artifact hash, and complete input fingerprint. 3) Strict validation deterministically rejects the fast profile, while the fast validator rejects full or tampered/stale artifacts. 4) Existing full current-source commands remain full and strict. 5) Fixture tests prove output/metadata isolation and validator separation. 6) Focused native OCaml, JS, C++ source, plugin-runtime, and macro-host checks are recorded. 7) The measured speedup and proof limitations are documented; README readiness bars remain evidence-based.

title: Split the C++ generator hotspot for faster native hxhx rebuilds
description: A clean instrumented hxhx emit at commit 15d53686 took 211 seconds after Haxe typing completed in about 2 seconds. Reflaxe spent 106.535 seconds on backend.cpp.CppTargetCore alone and generated a 12.2 MB OCaml module from the 26,920-line mixed-purpose Haxe class. This one class now owns over half of fresh compiler emission and slows every C++ compiler-source edit.
design: Extract coherent C++ representation, type-flow, rendering, support-class, and orchestration responsibilities into documented target-owned modules, starting with the largest bounded seam that has existing focused coverage. Do not move semantic operator binding into C++, invent a new backend-neutral IR, or replace one mega-file with another. Measure the same isolated emit before and after, and use the existing native plugin boundary where it lets unchanged compiler core and changed target code build independently. Exact full-compiler and release lanes keep the complete builtin target set until plugin equivalence is proved.
acceptance_criteria: 1) Record exact baseline commit, command, capacity, per-class generation time, generated bytes, and total wall time. 2) CppTargetCore has a substantial net responsibility and line-count reduction, with new modules documented and kept reviewable. 3) Comparable profiling shows a material reduction in CppTargetCore generation and fresh compiler wall time; no speed claim is made from saturated runs. 4) Focused C++ semantic/source-shape/runtime tests, current-source build, formatter, mega-file/architecture guards, and exact strict separation pass. 5) No backend-side abstract-operator rebinding, helper-name selection, parsed-body semantic reads, or release-proof shortcut is introduced. 6) Record whether the extracted C++ backend can be promoted to the shared native plugin artifact/loader contract; any host-specific shell remains thin and evidence-justified. 7) README Goals and North Star bars change only for real production-readiness movement.
close_reason: Completed the first measured hotspot extraction: CppTargetCore generation is 26% faster in the comparable full profile, source semantics remain unchanged, full current-source and bootstrap builds pass, strict fast/full separation holds, and all focused and repository guard evidence is recorded.

title: Make the hxhx edit-build-test loop fast and contention-aware
description: A fresh current-source build at b08b454b took 333 seconds in stage0 generation versus 251 seconds on the immediately preceding candidate, and the unchanged 480-second C++ Gate3 timed out after 482 seconds instead of reaching clang near 409 seconds. The host load was about 48 with several unrelated Haxe/Reflaxe builds consuming full cores. The current developer cache also binds to the whole commit/tree, so docs, tests, and bead-only changes can force a multi-minute compiler rebuild even when compiler inputs are identical. Shorten the ordinary edit-build-test loop without weakening exact release proof.
design: Measure host contention, stage0 Haxe generation, OCaml/Dune build, focused compiler execution, backend emission, and target-native compilation separately. Add an explicit resource-capacity preflight for heavy local proofs so extreme contention is reported and the run waits or stops before wasting the full timeout unless the caller deliberately overrides it. Add a developer-only current-source reuse path keyed by the real compiler/bootstrap input set so docs/tests/bead-only changes can reuse an identical compiler artifact. Keep validate-current-source-hxhx-bin.sh and all release/same-SHA evidence commit-bound. Document and expose one beginner-friendly fast loop: changed formatter and focused tests, compiler-input-aware binary reuse, focused native smoke, then one fresh unfiltered proof. Only optimize compiler/backend hot paths after stable uncontended phase evidence identifies them.
acceptance_criteria: 1) Reproducible phase evidence records commit, compiler-input digest, clean/incremental state, host CPU/load, competing compiler processes, command, and raw time. 2) A heavy local proof cannot silently consume its full timeout under extreme pre-existing contention; default behavior is deterministic, documented, and explicitly overridable. 3) A developer cache reuses the compiler across docs/tests/beads-only commits when the complete compiler/bootstrap input digest is unchanged, but invalidates for any relevant source, build configuration, runtime, snapshot, or toolchain change. 4) Strict current-source/release validation remains exact-commit and rejects the developer shortcut. 5) Fixture tests cover reuse, invalidation, contention policy, and strict separation. 6) Measured warm developer loops improve materially without slowing or weakening focused/full gates. 7) Beginner docs explain stage0, stage0-forbidden proof, fast versus decisive loops, and current Reflaxe lane readiness. 8) README Goals/North Star, cleanup, CI, and performance-owner evidence are reviewed honestly.

title: M22.12 — Gate M22 evidence and authorize the supported SDK claim
description: Build the artifact-verified aggregate for the declared M22 scope. The aggregate opens the actual per-form proof summaries, verifies same candidate, attempt, toolchain, service, ABI, target-core, plugin payload, and emitted-artifact identities, and only then emits the milestone marker. This bead owns the final support/no-go decision. Stock Haxe and hxhx loading the shared native Reflaxe plugin payload are required product lanes, not optional related research.
acceptance_criteria: 1) A scheduled or manual workflow runs the real declared execution, service-access, activation, and host matrix, including stock Haxe and hxhx loading the shared native plugin payload. 2) Per-lane summaries include exact candidate SHA, run ID and attempt, execution form, service-access form, activation form, host identity, stage0 policy, host fingerprint, service catalog digest, ABI versions, target-core identity, plugin payload digest, any loader-shell digest, emitted artifact digests, and runtime result. 3) Aggregate validation rejects missing, stale, synthetic, wrong-SHA, wrong-attempt, wrong-form, service-mismatch, ABI-mismatch, payload-digest mismatch, unjustified host packaging divergence, skipped, or failed proofs. 4) The identical plugin binary is preferred and must be attempted on the supported reference toolchain; any different loader shell requires an opened evidence record proving the exact OCaml/runtime incompatibility and the shared payload/core identity. 5) Stock-Haxe/hxhx plugin parity, hxhx plugin/builtin parity, and evaluated/native host-neutral parity are checked from artifacts, not job result strings. 6) The real-target proof and performance report are opened and validated. 7) The aggregate emits M22_REFLAXE_NATIVE_COMPILER_SDK:PASS only for the declared supported scope. 8) README, North Star, and public docs move from no-go to supported only after the aggregate passes for one exact candidate. 9) Written xhigh second-pass reviews are recorded before the support claim and parent epic closure.

title: M22.8 — Ship one stock-Haxe/hxhx native Reflaxe plugin ABI
description: Make native Reflaxe promotion a cross-host product capability. A Haxe-authored target such as reflaxe.ocaml must promote to one versioned native plugin payload that stock upstream Haxe and hxhx can both load and run. The identical binary artifact is the preferred and required design target. If an observed OCaml compiler/runtime/linker incompatibility makes one container impossible, permit only thin mechanically generated host loader shells around one shared ABI payload, with the incompatibility and payload identity proven. Never fork target semantics or maintain separate plugin implementations.
design: Define the plugin contract independently of either compiler's private AST and runtime objects. Both hosts expose the same immutable backend program/facts envelope, lifecycle, capability negotiation, diagnostics, resource, and output services. Prefer a stable C-compatible or otherwise cross-runtime representation where OCaml dynlink identity would couple the payload to one host. Keep stock-Haxe and hxhx loaders thin and conformance-tested. Treat different packaging as an evidence-gated fallback, not the default. Preserve the portable evaluated Reflaxe path, but make the native stock-Haxe plugin a required M22 product form rather than optional research.
acceptance_criteria: 1) One versioned native plugin ABI is specified for both stock Haxe and hxhx. 2) One promoted reflaxe.ocaml plugin payload is loaded unchanged by both hosts on the supported reference toolchain. 3) Both hosts expose the same typed service catalog, lifecycle, immutable program/facts schema, diagnostics, resources, and output contract. 4) Same-fixture conformance proves declaration identity, emitted artifacts, diagnostics, and runtime behavior agree across both hosts. 5) No private upstream-Haxe AST value, private hxhx object, mutable compiler context, helper-name convention, or target-specific semantic rebinding crosses the ABI. 6) ABI, schema, host, toolchain, target-core, and artifact digests fail fast on mismatch. 7) If identical binary loading is impossible, a written experiment records the exact OCaml/runtime constraint; only thin generated loader shells may differ, and they must open the same payload digest or reproducibly derived core digest. 8) Separate target implementations or semantic forks are forbidden. 9) Stock-Haxe native plugin packaging, install, upgrade, rollback, and trust boundaries are documented alongside hxhx. 10) M22 aggregate evidence treats stock-Haxe and hxhx plugin execution as required same-candidate lanes. 11) A written thinking:xhigh second-pass review precedes implementation closure and any public readiness increase.

title: Make Full1 timing files say which code and machine they measured
description: The heavy Full1 jobs already record how long each setup, build, and test phase takes. Today the downloaded timing file cannot identify the exact hxhx commit, GitHub run, computer class, or tool versions by itself, and its source field contains a machine-local absolute path. Make the timing report self-contained so a new contributor can understand and compare it without opening the workflow log or guessing where it came from.
design: Hard-cut the diagnostic timing summary to a self-describing v2 schema. Keep phase capture lightweight and report-only. Reuse the standard GitHub environment plus small local tool probes, normalize paths, and add one validator rather than copying provenance checks into every workflow. Do not change Full1 coverage, pass/fail rules, or performance thresholds.
acceptance_criteria: 1) Every v2 timing summary records the exact 40-character commit, tracked-source clean state at summary time, creation time, workflow/job, GitHub run ID and attempt when available, OS/architecture/CPU, and Node/Haxe/OCaml/Dune/Python versions with an explicit unavailable value when needed. 2) The summary keeps the raw phase rows and explains that their sum is measured phase time, not necessarily total job time. 3) No absolute local path appears in the report. 4) One validator rejects missing or malformed provenance, commit disagreement, inconsistent workflow/job rows, bad timestamps/durations/status/exit codes, and totals that disagree with the raw phases. 5) Focused fixtures cover local and GitHub-style reports plus the failure cases. 6) All heavy Full1 workflows continue to publish timing JSON/Markdown, and their workflow guard plus repository guards pass without weakening any gate. 7) One pushed exact-commit workflow produces an authentic v2 artifact that passes independent validation before closure. 8) Docs explain the result in beginner-friendly language; README Goals bars change only if production usability changes.
close_reason: V2 timing receipts now carry strict commit, run, machine, tool, raw-phase, and safe-path provenance; focused/full guards passed and exact-commit GitHub run 29303951143 produced three independently validated passing reports.

The total is labeled as measured phases only, not whole-job wall time. The validator rejects old/malformed schemas, missing provenance, candidate/checkout or phase/summary commit disagreement, mixed runs/jobs, invalid timestamps/durations, pass/exit contradictions, incorrect totals, release-looking evidence, and absolute paths. Local and GitHub-style synthetic fixtures pass. title: Measure how long a clean stage0-free hxhx build takes
description: A developer can already build a native hxhx executable from the committed OCaml bootstrap snapshot without asking the installed upstream Haxe compiler to compile it. We do not yet have a trustworthy, self-contained report for the wait or memory cost. Add a report-only benchmark that repeats this real build on one machine and proves every timing produced a usable native executable.
design: Use the existing stage0-forbidden build-hxhx path and fresh temporary build workspaces. Record build wall time and an honestly named peak-memory scope; do not present one process peak as total machine memory. Prefer a small reusable command-resource helper and the existing report conventions instead of embedding another large measurement engine in shell. No generated ML edits and no blocking threshold.
acceptance_criteria: 1) The measured command forbids stage0/upstream-Haxe use and produces a native .exe rather than bytecode; each accepted sample runs a small hxhx smoke and records the artifact digest. 2) At least three fresh-workspace repetitions can run sequentially on one machine, with preparation/cache/warmup meaning stated plainly. 3) A self-describing report records commit and clean state, timestamp, OS/architecture/CPU, Node/Haxe/OCaml/Dune versions, exact command/configuration, Dune-job/cache state, wall time, honestly scoped peak memory, and raw samples. 4) Validation rejects missing provenance, a bytecode artifact, cross-commit evidence, missing/failed samples, changed artifact bytes, and summaries that disagree with raw runs. 5) The benchmark remains diagnostic/report-only with no release threshold. 6) Focused fixtures, repository guards, and one clean local or same-runner CI proof pass. 7) Docs explain the result in beginner-friendly language, and README Goals bars change only if real production usability changes.
close_reason: Implemented and validated a self-contained report-only stage0-free native hxhx build benchmark with three clean samples per cache lane.

comments.author: Marcelo Serpa
comments.text: Measurement design: use two clearly named clean-workspace states. The cold lane disables Dune shared caching for every measured build. The warm-cache lane uses a private benchmark cache, primes it once without recording that timing, then measures fresh build workspaces against that same cache. Both lanes forbid stage0, demand a native .exe, smoke the result outside the timed build, and retain artifact digests. Peak memory will use a dedicated command-resource helper and be labeled as the operating system maximum for the completed build child hierarchy, not simultaneous whole-machine or exact tree-sum memory. This keeps the claim honest and makes cache state reproducible without clearing the developer global cache.

comments.author: Marcelo Serpa
comments.text: Implementation checkpoint: the new report-only runner forbids stage0 with an unusable Haxe sentinel, creates a fresh build workspace for every sample, requires a native .exe, and runs a target-list smoke before accepting the timing. It compares cache-disabled builds with a separately primed private Dune cache and deletes the private cache/build workspaces afterward. A dedicated Python helper records elapsed time and OS child-hierarchy peak RSS; the report keeps its honest memory boundary, bootstrap-snapshot digest, native artifact/resource/log/smoke digests, and raw samples. A dirty-tree one-repetition smoke at commit d2cb6a2c completed: cache-disabled 25929 ms / 1641536 KiB; cache-primed 26135 ms / 1649360 KiB. The private cache showed no speed benefit in this single smoke. These are wiring facts only, not baseline or speed evidence. Focused validator fixtures, the latency policy guard, shell/Node/Python syntax, and the previously landed plugin-report fixtures pass. GPT design escalation was skipped because the committed-snapshot build boundary was explicit and testable. No generated ML changed. README Goals progress bars unchanged because measurement capability is not production readiness.

title: Measure how long a real hxhx-built plugin takes to build and run
description: The current hxhx-native-reflaxe benchmark compiles and runs a normal Haxe application. That is useful target-runtime evidence, but it does not measure the target-author loop promised by the north star: turn Haxe-authored backend code into an OCaml plugin, load it into hxhx, compile a sample, and run the result. Add a report-only benchmark around the existing upstream-to-hxhx and hxhx-to-hxhx plugin proof paths so both routes are measured sequentially on the same machine.
acceptance_criteria: 1) A report-only runner measures the upstream-Haxe plugin-build baseline and the native hxhx-built plugin route sequentially on one machine, using the already-proven real plugin load and sample-runtime paths. 2) Preparing the hxhx executable is measured separately from the repeated plugin loop. 3) The report records commit, clean state, OS/CPU, Haxe/Node/OCaml/Dune versions, hxhx artifact kind and digest, commands, warmup rule, repetitions, and raw samples. 4) Every accepted sample includes a passing plugin proof summary and artifact digest; skipped, failed, or mismatched routes cannot become numeric evidence. 5) A validator and synthetic fixtures reject missing provenance, route mismatches, and summary/sample inconsistencies. 6) Docs clearly say the older hxhx-native-reflaxe workload is application compile/runtime evidence, while this new report measures plugin-author iteration. 7) Run a local or same-runner CI proof, record that evidence, and review README Goals status without changing its bars unless real user-facing readiness changes.

title: Make bootstrap regeneration stop the server it starts
description: The regeneration script sets an exit handler to stop its repo-owned Haxe server, but a later report-writing exit handler replaces it. In plain language: asking for a temporary server can leave it running. Combine both responsibilities so temporary means temporary.
design: Use one final exit handler that first preserves/writes the low-level report and then applies the existing repo-server cleanup policy. Add a fake-Haxe failure fixture so cleanup is proven without regenerating or editing any OCaml snapshot.
acceptance_criteria: 1) A regeneration run that starts a repo server without --keep-repo-server stops it on failure and removes PID/identity state. 2) Failure still writes its requested low-level report and preserves the original exit code. 3) --keep-repo-server remains an explicit opt-out from automatic stop. 4) Fast fixture leaves no process or tracked artifact behind. 5) Shell syntax and repository guards pass. 6) No generated ML changes.
close_reason: Bootstrap regeneration now preserves reports and cleans temporary repo servers through one tested exit handler.

comments.author: Marcelo Serpa
comments.text: Implemented one combined EXIT path: failure-report preservation runs first, then the existing temporary-server cleanup policy. The fixture starts a fake repo server, forces compile exit 23, proves status=error/exit_code=23 is written, proves the temporary server process and PID/identity files are removed, then separately proves --keep-repo-server still opts out until explicit stop. Validation: focused lifecycle fixture, shell syntax, full npm run ci:guards, git diff --check. No generated ML changed; README/North Star unchanged because this corrects maintenance/measurement plumbing, not production usability.

title: Keep the repo Haxe server matched to the selected compiler
description: The warm bootstrap run selected the direct upstream-Haxe binary after first using the Lix wrapper, but haxe-server.sh silently reused the wrapper-owned server. In plain language: the benchmark label changed while the compiler doing the server work did not. Make server reuse conditional on the selected Haxe executable and cover the behavior with a small fake-server test.
design: Store a normalized identity for the executable that started the repo-owned server. Reuse only when the live server identity matches the current HAXE_BIN; otherwise stop it and start a matching server. Keep this repo-owned and deterministic; do not inspect or modify generated OCaml output.
acceptance_criteria: 1) Starting twice with the same executable reuses the same server PID. 2) Starting with a different executable replaces the old server and records the new identity. 3) Stopping removes server identity state. 4) A fast fixture test uses fake Haxe executables and leaves no process behind. 5) Existing server start/status/stop behavior and shell syntax checks pass. 6) No generated ML file changes.
close_reason: Server reuse is now bound to the selected Haxe executable and covered by a process-lifecycle fixture.

comments.author: Marcelo Serpa
