The fake-server fixture proves same-binary reuse, different-binary replacement, old-process cleanup, status visibility, and state cleanup. Validation: npm run test:hxhx:haxe-server-identity; bash -n on helper/fixture; full npm run ci:guards; git diff --check. No generated ML changed. No README Goals or North Star docs change: this repairs measurement correctness but does not change production usability.

title: Record a completed warm bootstrap regeneration baseline
description: The bootstrap report is now trustworthy, but the only fresh GitHub run used the quick select-only check. Run the real warm regeneration path so a newcomer can see how long refreshing the committed OCaml snapshots currently takes on a known machine. Compare the Haxe launcher wrapper with its directly selected native upstream-Haxe binary in one job. This is a stage0 maintenance baseline; neither lane is the future stage0-free hxhx rebuild, and the result must not be presented as Full1 performance proof.
design: Use Utility / Bootstrap Regen Benchmark with scenario=warm, reps=2, verify=0, dune_jobs=auto, compare=1, and no policy override. The first authentic run proved that reusing one Haxe server across forced Reflaxe snapshot emissions is not a valid warm baseline: the second emit reused the first policy's server and produced incomplete generated output. Corrected meaning: warm reuses the existing generated-output directory, while every measured sample starts a fresh repo server matched to its selected wrapper/direct-upstream-Haxe policy and stops it afterward. Preserve older v1 artifacts as valid descriptions of their historical semantics. Do not edit generated ML.
acceptance_criteria: 1) One exact-commit GitHub run completes the warm scenario for both stage0 launcher policies on the same runner, with at least two raw repetitions per policy and Dune jobs held constant. 2) The downloaded hxhx.bootstrap-regen-benchmark.v1 artifact passes independent validation and records clean state, machine, toolchains, command/configuration, raw rows, source-report digests, and medians. 3) The evidence states plainly that wrapper/native here describe upstream-Haxe stage0 selection, not native hxhx. 4) Any failure, timeout, OOM, or changed tracked snapshot is classified and kept as honest evidence rather than hidden. 5) No speed threshold or README readiness increase is inferred from this first completed baseline. 6) No generated ML file is edited directly in the repository checkout.
close_reason: Exact-commit warm A/B regeneration evidence completed and independently validated; timings, machine/toolchains, raw samples, server isolation, and honest snapshot-drift caveat are recorded. Follow-up haxe_ocaml-8wzkc owns the separate generated-snapshot reconciliation question.

title: Make bootstrap regeneration benchmarks explain their own results
description: When a maintainer changes hxhx source, the repo may need to regenerate the committed OCaml bootstrap snapshots. The existing benchmark records timings, but someone opening the artifact must reconstruct which commit, machine, toolchains, and scenario produced them. Turn the existing output into one self-describing report so a newcomer can tell what was measured and later runs can be compared safely. This is measurement plumbing only: it must not invent a speed target or claim that bootstrap regeneration is production-ready.
design: Extend scripts/hxhx/bench-bootstrap-regen.sh through a dedicated Node report builder/validator; do not add a large inline Python or hand-edit generated OCaml files. Reuse the existing results.tsv and per-run JSON as primary measurements.
acceptance_criteria: 1) A machine-readable report records the exact commit and clean/dirty state, OS/CPU, Haxe/Node/OCaml/Dune versions, benchmark command/configuration, scenario meanings, and raw run rows. 2) The report summarizes each scenario/policy/Dune-jobs group with a median while retaining the raw per-run reports. 3) A validator and focused fixture tests reject missing provenance, mismatched row counts, invalid scenarios, and summaries that do not match raw samples. 4) The manual bootstrap benchmark workflow uploads and displays the report. 5) The report stays diagnostic/report-only; no blocking speed threshold is added. 6) Relevant guards pass, a small local scenario proves the real wiring, and README Goals bars either follow real user-facing readiness or are explicitly recorded unchanged.
close_reason: Self-describing bootstrap report is locally and remotely validated; exact-commit workflow run 29292003540 uploaded and rendered the report-only artifact.

title: Compare hxhx bytecode and native compiler speed on one GitHub machine
description: The first trusted hxhx.kpi.v2 report measured an OCaml bytecode compiler and showed roughly 5.2 seconds per small compile versus roughly 0.23 seconds for upstream Haxe. That is honest evidence, but it does not answer the user-facing question: how fast is the native hxhx executable? Add an opt-in, report-only comparison that builds and measures bytecode first and native second in one GitHub job, then publishes both raw reports plus a checked comparison without changing release thresholds.
acceptance_criteria: 1. One manual GitHub job measures bytecode and native hxhx for the same commit, runner/CPU, toolchains, commands, and repetition rules. 2. Both inputs are valid clean-source hxhx.kpi.v2 reports with raw samples. 3. A machine-readable comparator rejects a wrong artifact kind, cross-SHA input, runner/toolchain mismatch, or missing samples. 4. Requested native evidence fails honestly if build-hxhx falls back to bytecode; it is never labeled native. 5. The output reports bytecode/native medians and ratios as diagnostic evidence only; no threshold is weakened or invented. 6. A fresh manual GitHub artifact and run are recorded before closure. 7. README/North Star bars remain unchanged unless the measured result changes actual product usability. 8. No generated ML file is edited directly.
close_reason: Same-run Linux bytecode/native KPI evidence passed at commit 22385df1 with validated clean reports, raw samples, strict artifact-kind checks, and diagnostic-only ratios.

The runner now sets both, so either supported build route requests native. The corrected one-repetition, macro-disabled Apple M2 Pro run produced clean same-commit reports labeled ocaml-bytecode and native-executable and passed HXHX_KPI_ARTIFACT_COMPARISON:PASS. Diagnostic medians: OCaml portable/metal compile bytecode 5643/5536 ms versus native 359/358 ms; upstream control 157 ms in the bytecode pass and 189 ms in the native pass. Native/bytecode ratios were about 0.064 for those compile lanes and 0.09 for incremental lanes. This is one local sample, not a threshold or production-readiness claim. The complete ci:guards suite passed after the build-switch correction; focused fallback, cross-SHA, CPU/toolchain/config, missing-sample, and metric-shape cases also pass. README/North Star bars remain unchanged, and git status confirms no tracked/generated ML changes.

title: Give the external macro lane one reusable, non-recursive host
description: The weekly external-host lane starts a fresh macro-host build inside each compiler process. The unit step can use stage0 today, but the Gate 2 step disables stage0 and recursive auto-build then launches another macro-host build from inside the macro-host build. Define one explicit host lifecycle that a beginner can follow: build or obtain one candidate-bound host, record where it came from, and reuse it across unit, runci, and display checks without hidden fallback.
acceptance_criteria: 1) A written design names who builds the host, when, and which workflow steps reuse it. 2) Stage0 use is explicit and Full1 evidence has a stage0-free path. 3) A recursion regression proves macro-host compilation cannot auto-build another host. 4) Unit, runci, and display external-host checks use one authenticated same-SHA host artifact or executable. 5) Inproc remains an independent comparison lane. 6) Fresh aggregate evidence passes with no required fallback or skip. 7) A GPT 5.5 Pro architecture review or equivalent written xhigh second pass is recorded before implementation and closure.
close_reason: Verified one reusable, candidate-bound, stage0-forbidden external macro host in exact-commit two-mode aggregate 29334023225; project-defined macro loading remains separate under haxe_ocaml-vhk47.3.

comments.author: Marcelo Serpa
comments.text: PRODUCT PRIORITY CONFIRMED — Tooling speed and native-level performance are first-class product requirements, alongside compiler customizability and embeddability. The North Star wording further requires the performance class of well-designed hand-written OCaml, Go, or Rust compiler implementations on equivalent workloads. Future work must therefore treat a slow safe fallback as diagnosis, not completion, and must make the ordinary fast path correct, inspectable, and reproducible. This clarifies priority; README/North Star readiness bars do not change from wording alone.

title: M22 — Shared stock-Haxe/hxhx Native Reflaxe Plugin SDK
description:
Turn the completed Reflaxe promotion foundations into a supported Haxe-first compiler-authoring platform. A target author must be able to prototype with portable Reflaxe, keep one host-neutral target core in ordinary Haxe, compile that core to native OCaml through reflaxe.ocaml, and package one versioned native plugin payload that stock upstream Haxe and hxhx can both load. hxhx may also link the same target core as a builtin. The identical plugin binary is the design target and must be attempted on the supported reference toolchain. If measured OCaml compiler, runtime, linker, or loader constraints make one container impossible, only thin mechanically generated host loader shells may differ; they must open the same payload or reproducibly derived native core and may not contain target semantics.

This epic owns backend and target authoring after a host has parsed, resolved, typed, run the supported macro lifecycle, and frozen the backend-facing program. It does not make Reflaxe own the parser, resolver, typer, module graph, macro lifecycle, baseline diagnostics, or core compiler semantics. It does not authorize a raw mutable compiler-context escape hatch or pre-backend phase hooks.

The product model keeps three independent dimensions: execution form (evaluated or native), service access (host-neutral or capability-integrated), and activation or packaging (stock-Haxe plugin, hxhx plugin, or hxhx builtin). Named presets may combine those dimensions, but they do not replace the existing OCaml code-generation profile ocaml_profile=portable|metal. Both plugin hosts implement one ABI and one host-neutral baseline. hxhx can advertise additional typed services through that same versioned capability catalog. A plugin that requires a service a host does not provide fails before execution; it does not switch to a separate implementation.

An unsafe internal exact-host adapter may exist only as quarantined research. It cannot replace the supported shared ABI, shared payload, or stock-Haxe plugin product lane.
design:
1. Native execution and privileged capability are separate. reflaxe.ocaml supplies native execution; each host supplies a versioned service catalog.
2. Stock Haxe and hxhx implement one native plugin ABI and host-neutral baseline. The same promoted plugin payload is the required product target for both.
3. Identical binary packaging is preferred and must be attempted on the supported reference toolchain. Different loader shells are an evidence-gated fallback only for a demonstrated OCaml compiler, runtime, linker, or loader incompatibility. Shells remain thin, generated where practical, and contain no target semantics.
4. One semantic target core. Stock-Haxe plugin, hxhx plugin, and hxhx builtin are activation or packaging choices. Host-neutral evaluated and native paths share target semantics unless an explicitly declared capability-integrated feature requires more services.
5. Execution form, service access, activation or packaging, and the existing OCaml portable|metal code-generation profile are independent dimensions.
6. Data, services, and pre-backend phase providers are distinct. Stable immutable program facts belong in a backend program or facts envelope; host-owned actions belong in services. Pre-backend influence stays with Stage4 or the customization and variation owner unless a separate xhigh decision changes ownership.
7. No general compiler context. Expose semantic snapshots and capability-limited actions, not parser or typer records, private OCaml values, host object identity, or mutable global state.
8. Batch across native boundaries. Prefer immutable snapshots and coarse calls. No per-expression FFI service chatter.
9. Typed and versioned negotiation. Requirements distinguish required semantic services, optional optimizations, and optional tooling. Missing semantic requirements fail before backend execution.
10. Conditionals stay at the edge. Host-specific externs, transports, loaders, and preset selection live in adapters or composition roots. A guard prevents host-condition branches in shared lowering and printer code.
11. No speculative universal IR. Strengthen only the minimum backend envelope and facts required by at least two backends or one real promoted target plus a builtin backend.
12. ABI representation must be proven. Do not pass either compiler private ASTs or assume generated Haxe interface and OCaml object identity survive dynlink boundaries. Prefer a versioned cross-runtime representation, immutable snapshots, and opaque host handles unless direct typed-object passing is independently proven compatible.
13. Native plugins are trusted code. Document process and filesystem trust. Out-of-process sandboxing is future transport work, not an M22 blocker.
14. Evidence precedes claims. No README readiness increase or supported-SDK language until same-candidate artifacts prove both plugin hosts, the declared execution forms, payload identity, packaging, services, and behavior.
15. The first semantic candidate is a read-only batched reachability and retention snapshot. It may describe the final backend-visible retained set and stable reasons or IDs, but M22 does not grant target code authority to change frontend or DCE reachability. Portable fallback remains explicit keep or root declarations or fail-fast behavior; the exact contract must be proven by M22.6.
acceptance_criteria: 1) One nontrivial Haxe-authored target core is exercised without hand-rewritten lowering in an upstream-Haxe Reflaxe evaluated form, a stock-Haxe native plugin, an hxhx native plugin, and an hxhx builtin. 2) One versioned native plugin ABI is implemented by stock Haxe and hxhx, and one promoted reflaxe.ocaml plugin payload is loaded unchanged by both on the supported reference toolchain. 3) Identical plugin binary packaging is attempted and is the passing default. If it is proven impossible, only thin host loader shells may differ; evidence must name the exact OCaml runtime, compiler, linker, or loader incompatibility and prove the shared payload or reproducibly derived core identity. 4) Plugin and builtin wrappers consume the same target core and agree for the declared scope; evaluated and native host-neutral paths also agree unless an explicitly declared integrated feature is enabled. 5) A typed, versioned host-service contract classifies required-semantic, optional-optimization, and optional-tooling requirements, and missing required services fail before emission. 6) At least one real capability gap is closed with a privileged immutable semantic fact or service; stock-Haxe behavior has a proven fallback or fails clearly and never approximates correctness-critical data. 7) BackendContext remains deterministic invocation configuration with copy and freeze semantics; services and facts use a separate request boundary. 8) Backend ABI, backend program version, macro API version, host-service API version, manifest schema, service-access preset, target-core identity, payload digest, loader-shell digest where applicable, and host or toolchain compatibility are checked before plugin execution. 9) Host conditionals remain confined to adapters, transport, loaders, optimized implementations, and composition roots, enforced by a guard. 10) Parser, resolver, typer, macro lifecycle, and baseline diagnostic ownership do not import Reflaxe framework APIs. 11) Stock-Haxe plugin, hxhx plugin, and hxhx builtin execution prove artifact and runtime parity on a repo-owned fixture and one real compiler family; external copyleft sources remain fetched and pinned. 12) Native target-author iteration is measured by phase and includes a direct OCaml or native baseline only where genuinely comparable. 13) Packaging, rebuild and cache keys, provenance, support matrix, migration, diagnostics, ABI compatibility, loader-shell fallback, and trust boundaries are documented. 14) An artifact-derived aggregate emits M22_REFLAXE_NATIVE_COMPILER_SDK:PASS only for one declared same-candidate scope after written xhigh second-pass reviews.
notes: Accepted OCaml target-core checkpoint 2026-07-18: semantic convergence means both hosts adapt into one small typed OCaml-lowering core, not that M22 owns an OCaml or cross-target representation IR. Equivalent normalized inputs must eventually yield equal representation, lowered-program, runtime, dependency, export, syntax, and behavior evidence. The current Stage3 EmitterStage delegation is not semantic convergence and must lose target-lowering ownership at hard cutover. One payload on the pinned reference toolchain remains the product goal; this checkpoint does not promise dynlink compatibility across arbitrary OCaml compiler versions.

comments.author: Marcelo Serpa
comments.text:
XHIGH SECOND-PASS AMENDMENT — 2026-07-18

1. Human product decision: ACCEPTED. M22 now requires one versioned native Reflaxe plugin ABI and one promoted payload usable by stock Haxe and hxhx. M22.8 (haxe_ocaml-c4czv) is P0 and blocks M22.12; the stock-Haxe lane is no longer optional research.
2. ABI versus packaging: PASS. The ABI, payload, target-core identity, semantic decisions, diagnostics, resources, and outputs are shared requirements. One identical plugin binary is the default design and must be attempted on the supported reference toolchain. Different packaging is not presumed.
3. OCaml compatibility caveat: BOUNDED. A different host loader shell is allowed only after an experiment identifies the exact OCaml compiler, runtime, linker, or loader incompatibility. The shell must open the same payload digest or reproducibly derived native-core digest. It cannot contain target lowering, printing, mutation, result semantics, or another target implementation.
4. Host capability asymmetry: PASS. Both hosts implement the same catalog and negotiation protocol and provide the host-neutral baseline. hxhx may advertise additional typed compiler facts or services. If a plugin requires a capability stock Haxe lacks, stock Haxe fails before target execution; the payload does not branch to a weaker semantic implementation.
5. Compiler ownership and bootstrap circularity: PASS. The prior boundary remains unchanged. Parser, resolver, typer, module graph, macro lifecycle, and baseline diagnostics do not import Reflaxe framework APIs. M22 starts after the backend-facing program is frozen. Using reflaxe.ocaml to compile ordinary Haxe-authored hxhx sources remains distinct from making the compiler core depend on Reflaxe APIs.
6. ABI safety: PASS. Neither private upstream-Haxe AST objects nor private hxhx objects cross the plugin ABI. The plan prefers versioned immutable program/facts data and coarse service calls. Direct OCaml object identity or dynlink compatibility must be proven, not assumed.
7. Current truth versus future hard cutover: PASS. Current manifest-v1 upstream eval-host and hxhx native artifacts remain host-specific and continue to record crossHostBinaryCompatibility=false. The plan does not relabel those artifacts. M22 must hard-cut to the new ABI after implementation and migration evidence.
8. Evidence and claims: PASS. M22.12 must open same-candidate stock-Haxe plugin, hxhx plugin, and hxhx builtin artifacts, compare payload and optional loader-shell digests, and reject missing, stale, ABI-mismatched, semantically divergent, or unjustifiably repackaged lanes. README now labels the shared plugin as planning-only.
9. Documentation and readiness: PASS. README, North Star, promotion matrix, M22 plan, upstream integration decision, host-adapter guide, beginner promotion guide, current-capability snapshot, glossary, and stage0 policy distinguish current capability from planned architecture. Existing production-readiness bars and overall north-star bar are unchanged; the new shared-plugin row is [#---------] because the requirement is planned but not implemented.
10. Prior review relationship: this amendment supersedes item 6 and the optional-M22.8 portion of item 8 in the 2026-07-15 review. The earlier ownership, Full1 priority, no-raw-context, no-universal-IR, required-semantics, and evidence-before-claims conclusions remain in force.

Review result: accept the revised M22 planning contract and dependency graph. This authorizes architecture and future implementation ownership only. It does not establish a stock-Haxe native target plugin, cross-host binary compatibility, SDK support, or any release/readiness increase.

XHIGH PRODUCT-SCOPE SECOND PASS — 2026-07-19

The AI-assisted promotion principle is accepted with a bounded interpretation. M22 remains a compiler/target SDK; it does not become a generic application framework. Its authentic compiler workload is intentionally a hard stress test of the broader source-preserving Haxe model. The same economics can apply to any Haxe software: preserve the Haxe implementation, let a mature Reflaxe target supply the bulk native translation, and concentrate agent work on reusable semantic, interop, packaging, and performance gaps instead of maintaining a ground-up target-language rewrite.

Closure evidence under haxe_ocaml-bxwut, haxe_ocaml-i69n4, and haxe_ocaml-zof2e must include a migration receipt that separates retained Haxe source, target-specific Haxe, handwritten native adapter/raw code, reusable target fixes, behavior parity, iteration/build cost, and comparable native quality. comments.text:
PRODUCT-SCOPE CHECKPOINT — 2026-07-19

The source-preserving native-promotion thesis applies to ordinary Haxe applications, libraries, tools, servers, and plugins, not only compiler workloads. The durable model keeps Haxe source and tests authoritative, lets reflaxe.ocaml perform the broad translation, and uses AI-assisted work for the bounded remainder: reusable compiler/runtime gaps, typed native adapters, packaging, diagnostics, and measured hot paths. Generated OCaml is never the maintained patch surface.

Any future claim that Haxe performs most of the port must be backed by a migration receipt: retained target-neutral Haxe, target-specific Haxe, handwritten native and raw escape-hatch code, reusable target gaps closed, behavior parity, generated-code quality, build/iteration cost, native performance, and maintenance cost against a credible rewrite baseline. Compiler promotion is the demanding proof case, not the product boundary. This planning clarification adds no current standalone capability, does not expand the declared 1.0 scope, and leaves README readiness unchanged.

title: Make OCaml target-AST runtime scans stack-safe
description:
The current-source hxhx build now deterministically reaches a Haxe-side stack overflow while
reflaxe.ocaml scans the generated OCaml syntax tree for runtime-module references. The scan uses
`OcamlASTTraversal.walkExprPre`, which recursively calls itself once per nested OCaml expression.
Adding one ordinary Haxe expression variant enlarged the generated compiler enough to cross the
host call-stack limit; no invalid source program or cyclic target tree is involved.

Why this matters:

- A correct compiler build must not depend on whether a large generated expression happens to fit
  within the host Haxe process call stack.
- Runtime dependency discovery is a consistency check over an already-built tree. It should handle
  large compiler programs predictably and should not require users to increase process stack limits.
- The full current-source build is the gate needed to validate the null-safe field parser fix against
  the upstream macro workload, so this infrastructure defect blocks ordinary compiler iteration.

Implement an explicit work stack for deterministic pre-order walking of expressions, patterns, and
types. Preserve the existing authoritative immediate-child schema and event order. Keep tree mapping
recursive unless evidence shows that it also crosses the limit; the observed failure is specifically
the read-only runtime-usage walk.

Acceptance:

1. A focused deeply nested expression fixture overflows neither the expression walk nor runtime usage
   collection.
2. Existing walk/fold ordering and constructor-coverage tests remain unchanged and green.
3. The current-source hxhx build advances past `RuntimeUsageCollector` without increasing the process
   stack limit or skipping runtime validation.
4. Generated OCaml behavior and runtime-module selection remain unchanged for existing focused tests.
5. The fix is documented as stack-safety work, not as added language support or release readiness.
close_reason: Closed

title: Bound Beads history before it consumes developer disk
description: The local issue database now occupies about 724 MiB, including roughly 565 MiB of Dolt data and 113 MiB of backup data. All 3,074 database commits are newer than the default 30-day compaction window, so normal maintenance reports nothing to compact even though the shared development volume has less than 1 GiB free. This makes issue tracking itself a material source of disk pressure and can slow or block compiler work. Define a backup-first, non-destructive retention policy, measure the real space recovered by supported Beads maintenance, and add a read-only warning before the database reaches unsafe size again. Keep current issue contents and tracked JSONL intact; do not delete closed issues merely to save space.
design: Use supported Beads backup, history compaction, and Dolt garbage-collection commands rather than deleting database files. Prove the backup is current and restorable before rewriting history. Require enough temporary headroom for the rewrite, preserve a documented recent-history window, compare issue counts/content digests before and after, and leave routine diagnostics read-only. Coordinate this with the Git-storage and artifact-cleanup doctors so each reports its own storage owner instead of claiming whole-volume cleanup.
acceptance_criteria: A dry run explains retained versus compactable history and required headroom; a verified backup exists before maintenance; supported maintenance completes without losing current issue records or tracked JSONL; before/after disk use and command duration are recorded; repeated maintenance is bounded; a read-only doctor warns early enough to act safely; focused tests and repository guards pass.
close_reason: Verified storage repair and durable byte-based recurrence warnings

comments.author: Marcelo Serpa
comments.text:
Diagnostic checkpoint, 2026-07-20.

Practical outcome: the read-only Beads storage check no longer says everything is healthy merely because there is one active database. Before this change, it reported `PASS` while the active database used 552.1 MiB, local backup data used 110.6 MiB, and the complete `.beads` directory used 725.7 MiB. There were no sibling or dropped databases, so the old check missed the actual growth.

The doctor now asks for review when the active database reaches 256 MiB or all local Beads state reaches 512 MiB. Those values are deliberately earlier than the observed recurrence: after the previous reviewed maintenance, the active database was about 67 MiB and the complete store about 217 MiB. It also reports filesystem space and conservative maintenance headroom, with a plain warning that a single database can accumulate a large local change history.

A deterministic fixture simulates 300,000 KiB of active history and 600,000 KiB total storage without allocating a large real file. It proves both warning reasons, the beginner-readable explanation, JSON threshold/headroom fields, and a byte-identical database tree before and after the check. Existing skip, healthy, sibling, dropped, missing-active, and malformed-metadata cases remain green. The live doctor now exits with review-required status 2 and names `active_database_storage,total_beads_storage` instead of returning `PASS`.

During the first fixture run, the system returned `ENOSPC` while creating an empty temporary directory. APFS subsequently reclaimed purgeable space and reported about 16 GiB available; no project data was deleted to cause the recovery. This makes headroom visible but does not authorize live compaction. A verified restorable backup, isolated trial, before/after record checks, and supported Beads maintenance are still required before this bead can close.

Focused Beads and Git doctor fixtures, local-path guard, native-iteration-latency guard, Node syntax checks, and diff checks pass. title: Make cleanup reliable under critical disk pressure
description: The repository cleanup command failed with 'no space left on device' while trying to create its own temporary candidate file, even though cleanup was the required recovery action. After manually deleting one ignored 67 MB build directory, the command worked, but safe/deep modes still ignored roughly 700 MB of stale .artifacts evidence. Make cleanup capable of reclaiming space when the filesystem is nearly full, and give old generated evidence an explicit retention/cleanup contract instead of requiring hand deletion.
design: Keep cleanup deterministic and fail-safe. Avoid needing writable temporary storage before the first bounded reclaim, or provide a minimal emergency path that streams known safe candidates. Add an explicit age/ownership policy for ignored .artifacts evidence; do not delete committed bootstrap snapshots, active build directories, current proof artifacts, or files with a declared retention owner. Report what is protected and why. Test both low-space setup failure and stale-evidence handling without filling a real disk.
acceptance_criteria: 1. A focused fixture simulates temporary-file creation failure and proves a bounded safe cleanup can still reclaim a known ignored artifact. 2. Stale .artifacts and generic .tmp evidence have an explicit age/ownership retention policy and dry-run inventory. 3. Active build leases and retained proof artifacts remain protected. 4. Safe, deep, and emergency behavior are documented in beginner-friendly language. 5. Disk usage and cleanup latency are measured before/after. 6. README Goals and North Star impact is recorded.
close_reason: The low-space cleanup path is bounded and fixture-proven, exact Q3 Core and release verification passed, and v0.23.3 was published from the verified candidate.

comments.author: Marcelo Serpa
comments.text: LOW-SPACE REPRODUCTION — On 2026-07-20, available space fell from about 1.4 GiB to 369–457 MiB while this checkout had no heavy local build running. 'npm run clean:dry-run -- --verbose' succeeded but found only one 4 KiB safe candidate, even though this checkout retained 36 MiB under ignored .artifacts; the wider workspace also contained a separate 920 MiB .tmp tree outside this repository's ownership. This confirms two requirements: cleanup must remain usable when temp-file creation is at risk, and it must explain which local evidence is retained rather than silently reporting almost nothing reclaimable. Do not delete another repository's artifacts from this tool; cross-repository ownership needs an explicit coordinator.

This explains why filesystem availability fluctuated independently of the 35.3 MiB local .artifacts inventory. The repository command must keep reporting its true bounded impact rather than claiming whole-volume cleanup.

title: Do not classify generated program modules as OCaml runtime sources
description: The fail-closed runtime checker currently treats every structured OCaml reference whose module name begins with Hx plus an uppercase letter as a compatibility-runtime request. When hxhx or the macro host is compiled, ordinary generated program modules such as HxClassDecl match that spelling and are rejected because they correctly do not exist in the locked runtime-source catalog. Preserve unknown-runtime failure behavior while distinguishing compiler-owned compatibility modules from modules generated from the current Haxe program.
design: Build a deterministic set of target module names owned by the current generated program and use it when interpreting structured target references. A name that resolves to a program-owned module is a normal program dependency, not a runtime request. Runtime modules remain validated against the locked manifest. Reject ambiguous output ownership or collisions instead of guessing. Keep the target-syntax scan as a migration consistency check; do not weaken the semantic runtime ledger or accept every unknown Hx-prefixed name.
acceptance_criteria: 1) Generated program modules with Hx-style names are not requested from the compatibility-runtime manifest. 2) Misspelled or unknown compatibility-runtime requests still fail before packaging. 3) The distinction uses declared program/module ownership rather than a broad name exclusion. 4) Focused positive and negative tests cover collisions and deterministic behavior. 5) Macro-host integration and strict plugin matrix pass on the exact pushed revision. 6) README Goals and North Star readiness impact is recorded.
close_reason: Program-owned generated OCaml modules are now separated from the locked compatibility runtime without weakening unknown-runtime failures; focused tests and exact pushed macro-host/plugin/portable evidence pass.

title: Prevent concurrent oversized Haxe formatter hangs
description: The formatter guard isolates very large Haxe files, but its generic worker queue can start all of those expensive formatter processes together. On the current 804-file tree, this made the C++ and source backend mega-files compete on an already busy development host, while a one-heavy-worker experiment was safe but took 264.5 seconds. Keep normal chunks parallel, cap oversized-file work below the total worker count, and make a genuinely stuck child fail with an actionable timeout instead of hanging indefinitely.
design: Extend the existing deterministic formatter plan rather than replacing the official formatter. Mark oversized tasks explicitly. Use at most two heavy workers by default, always reserve capacity for ordinary files, and allow a constrained host to lower the heavy cap. Give each formatter task a hard deadline, terminate its complete child-process group on timeout, and preserve stable result ordering. Fixture tests use controlled asynchronous work so concurrency and cleanup claims do not depend on slow real files.
acceptance_criteria: 1. Fixture tests prove ordinary tasks still run in parallel while oversized work never consumes every configured worker. 2. The default uses no more than two oversized workers, and an explicit one-worker heavy cap remains deterministic. 3. A timed-out formatter task terminates and reports the exact files and timeout without leaving a child process. 4. Result ordering, failure propagation, and HX_FORMAT_JOBS=1 behavior remain deterministic. 5. The real npm run guard:hx-format completes without a serial fallback and its measured time is recorded. 6. Documentation explains the policy in beginner-readable language, and README/North Star readiness is reviewed.
notes:
A first full measurement with one oversized worker passed all 804 files, but took 264.528 seconds under load average above 25 on a 12-core shared development host. The four large files alone took 124.669s, 81.184s, 22.656s, and 36.017s, while ordinary chunks completed in at most 15.990s. This proves a one-lane policy is safe but unnecessarily serial. The revised default caps heavy work at two workers and reserves the remaining capacity for ordinary files; HX_FORMAT_OVERSIZED_JOBS=1 remains available for constrained-host diagnosis.
FINAL MEASUREMENT — bounded heavy parallelism. The revised two-heavy-worker default passed all 804 tracked Haxe files in 113.653 seconds while the same shared 12-core host remained above load average 24. The one-heavy-worker comparison took 264.528 seconds, so the normal path is 57% faster without returning to the old all-mega-files-at-once schedule. The largest task took 107.345s; no task approached the 240s deadline. Fixture evidence also proves the one-heavy-worker override, serial mode, stable result ordering, ordinary-file parallelism, and process-group cleanup after a forced timeout. README Goals and North Star bars remain unchanged because this repairs developer-tool reliability and latency without changing a supported compiler capability.
close_reason: The full formatter guard now reserves capacity for ordinary files, limits oversized work to two tasks by default, supports a one-heavy-worker diagnostic override, and kills an entire formatter process group after a configurable deadline. Controlled fixtures and two real 804-file measurements prove the revised path is deterministic, leak-free, and 57% faster than the safe serial-heavy prototype. README Goals and North Star bars remain unchanged.

title: Keep Reflaxe program revisions stable across irrelevant macro-local renumbering
description: Reflaxe currently hashes Haxe's printed typed-expression form to identify the final target program. A mechanical refactor inside the target compiler changed every focused fixture's program revision even though the user program, generated OCaml, representation choices, and runtime behavior were unchanged. Repeated builds of the same candidate are deterministic, so this is not random output, but the revision appears to include process-global local-variable numbering or another compiler-internal detail. Investigate and canonicalize the target-neutral Reflaxe revision model so it identifies the normalized user program rather than irrelevant numbering from macro or target implementation code.
design: Keep two identities separate: the host-program revision describes normalized target-selected Haxe declarations and typed bodies, while the target-pipeline/configuration revision describes the Reflaxe target implementation and settings. Normalize local identities within each function or use adapter-supplied stable identities; do not erase resolved fields, types, ordering, or behavior-sensitive structure. Implement any Reflaxe framework change in the fullofcaffeine/reflaxe fork through a separate worktree and a detailed signed PR. The existing GPT-5.6 lifecycle and native-power reviews provide the required second-pass architecture boundary.
acceptance_criteria: 1. A focused target-neutral Reflaxe test perturbs compiler or macro local numbering without changing the selected user program and proves the program revision stays equal. 2. A real semantic body, type, declaration, retention, or access change still changes the program revision. 3. Target-pipeline changes remain separately versioned and invalidate target plans when required. 4. Repeated fresh and compiler-server builds are deterministic and stale revisions fail closed. 5. Upstream-Haxe and future hxhx adapters can produce equivalent normalized revisions without host object identity, absolute paths, or source offsets. 6. The Reflaxe change lands through the documented fork worktree/PR process and existing target integrations remain green.
close_reason: Merged, pinned, and verified stable Reflaxe ProgramRevision behavior on Linux and macOS

comments.author: Marcelo Serpa
comments.text:
THINKING:XHIGH IMPLEMENTATION SECOND PASS — 2026-07-21

Practical problem: Reflaxe gives the selected Haxe program a content hash so targets can reject stale cached plans. That hash currently includes Haxe's process-wide local-variable numbers. A local such as `value` can therefore be printed as `value(5378)` in one otherwise identical typed body and `value(5380)` in another merely because unrelated macro code was typed first. A direct Haxe 4.3.7 probe reproduced this: the two complete typed-expression renderings differed only in those IDs. This explains how a compiler-side refactor changed every focused program revision without changing generated OCaml or runtime behavior.

Chosen boundary: keep the existing exact working-body revision unchanged, and add a separate program-body digest for `ProgramRevision`. The working-body revision answers whether a plan still belongs to the exact mutable body observed during one preprocessing run. The program revision answers whether two normalized, target-selected Haxe programs mean the same thing across fresh requests. Conflating these identities would either keep the current cache churn or weaken the exact in-request stale-plan check.

Minimum implementation: render the same complete typed expression currently used by Reflaxe, then rewrite only the numeric ID inside Haxe's structured `[Local name(id):...]` and `[Var name(id):...]` records. Assign small function-local ordinals in first structural occurrence order. Use a single scanner rather than broad regular expressions or pretty-printed source. This preserves Haxe semantic types, resolved field owners and access forms, operators, control structure, declaration names, metadata, and literal values already present in the detailed rendering. Program declarations and fields continue to be sorted and hashed exactly as today. The target pipeline/configuration revision remains separate and still invalidates target plans when the target implementation changes.

Required tests: prove that typing the same expression before and after an unrelated local allocation yields different raw Haxe renderings but equal normalized program-body digests. Also prove that a changed literal/operator, semantic type, resolved field access, or retained module changes the revision. Existing tests continue to cover callback-order independence, exact-body replacement/in-place mutation, request-local caches, trace determinism, and stale-plan failure.

Invariants: normalization is function-local and deterministic; it never uses source offsets, absolute paths, host object identity, or local names as the binding identity; distinct shadowed locals remain distinct because their original IDs map to distinct local ordinals; only the unstable numeric IDs are discarded; real typed-tree changes still change the program revision; exact body revisions remain strict; and upstream-Haxe/future-hxhx adapters can later supply the same normalized body contract without importing target-specific rules.

Rejected shortcuts: hashing pretty-printed Haxe source loses resolved type and field-access detail; deleting every number could erase literals and type information; regex replacement risks touching user strings or unrelated compiler data; using local names merges shadowed variables; retaining raw IDs preserves the bug; and canonicalizing `FunctionBodyRevision` at the same time would unnecessarily broaden a program-cache fix into the in-request lifecycle guard.

This written audit applies the two accepted GPT-5.6 architecture reviews to the concrete implementation seam. It authorizes the bounded target-neutral Reflaxe fork change and focused tests, not a universal typed-expression IR, host wire format, or readiness increase. The change must use the isolated fork worktree and a detailed signed fork PR.

`thinking:xhigh` is this repository's internal risk label for work where a wrong architecture or release decision could create misleading evidence. It is defined under “Thinking Levels (Bead Labels)” in `AGENTS.md`.

That review checks the evidence, ownership boundary, invariants, rejected shortcuts, and tests. It can be an independent Oracle review or a written design audit in the Bead. It does not mean that implementation or validation has already passed.

For this issue, the two existing GPT-5.6 architecture reviews establish the broad boundary, and the preceding note applies that boundary to the narrower local-number normalization change. The earlier all-caps heading was an internal checklist label and should have led with this explanation.

comments.author: Marcelo Serpa
comments.text:
Implementation and current-source proof (2026-07-21):

Practical problem:

- Upstream `vendor/haxe/tests/runci/targets/Flash.hx` contains `final possibleStrings = unexpectedStrings?.copy() ?? [];`.
- The parser tokenized `?` and `.` separately, then treated `?` as the start of a ternary expression. It reached `copy` while still looking for the ternary `:` and failed with `Expected ':'`.

Implemented behavior:

- Added a structured null-safe field expression that keeps the receiver and field name distinct from ordinary field access. The parser accepts adjacent `?.` and deliberately does not accept spaced `? .` as null-safe access.
- Typed bodies retain that structure instead of hiding it in an opaque source-shaped leaf. The typed result is nullable, including while its inner result type is still unknown.
- Macro conversion maps the access to Haxe's public `ExprDef.EField(..., Safe)` form. C++, JavaScript, Neko, Python, and PHP macro-quote builders preserve the same public access kind.
- JavaScript runtime emission uses native optional chaining without evaluating the receiver twice.
- OCaml Stage3 and Neko runtime emission reject the not-yet-lowered operation explicitly. C++/source paths expose an explicit kind or unsupported diagnostic rather than losing the source syntax. Full shared evaluation/runtime lowering is linked as `haxe_ocaml-0dzoi` and is not claimed by this parser bead.
- Every ordinary expression traversal found during the full build was updated. The first full build correctly exposed a missing `ExprMacroExpander` case; that exhaustive switch was fixed before the successful build.

Focused evidence:

- Parser exact-shape, complete Flash-like two-statement snippet, unsupported-scan, and whitespace-negative cases pass.
- Typed-body structure and nullable result checks pass.

THINKING:XHIGH SECOND-PASS AND HOSTED CLOSURE — 2026-07-20

A fresh implementation audit confirms the promised ownership boundary, not only passing output. OcamlPlaceAssignmentPlanner is constructed only by OcamlPlacePlanSealer, which runs from the final expression preprocessor. CompilerInit appends that finalizer after every generic rewrite. The finalizer replaces each temporary early marker with one final origin, plans every admitted field/static/array assignment or update, validates the result, and seals the exact ClassFuncData body revision. OcamlPlacePlanRegistry is cleared for each program revision, rejects duplicate origins or late additions, and compares function/program/body/pipeline revisions again before syntax construction.

OcamlBuilder no longer receives a TypedExpr and metadata to decide the place operation. Its small change reads a final origin, requires the current sealed function binding, and delegates to a lowerer that can only resolve and emit the already-selected plan. Unknown passes are rejected by the Reflaxe lifecycle declaration; known structural passes must preserve the family; the early-to-final transition must provide a complete one-to-one replacement map. Final validation rejects leftover early markers, missing plans, changed bodies, and mismatched inventories before OCaml output. The late-mutation fixture proves that failure path.

No architecture stop condition was found: there is no builder rebinding, legacy fallback, arbitrary metadata preservation, Dynamic/raw/Obj.magic recovery, second production path, or new mega-file subsystem. Runtime module copying is still mechanically requested by the plan emitter; the broader source-to-runtime capability ledger remains explicitly owned by haxe_ocaml-0uwin and is not claimed by this slice.

title: Add revisioned semantic-envelope lifecycle to Reflaxe
description: Reflaxe owns the mutable ClassFuncData container and ordered expression-preprocessor list that currently allow a target-owned place envelope to disappear silently. Add a narrow target-neutral lifecycle contract in the Reflaxe repository so opted-in targets can bind semantic artifacts to immutable function/body revisions, declare whether each preprocessor preserves, replaces, invalidates, or rejects an opaque family, and validate ownership before target compilation.
design: Work only in a separate clean Reflaxe worktree and land through a detailed pull request in the maintained fullofcaffeine/reflaxe fork. Synchronize the fork with SomeRanDev/reflaxe first and follow docs/00-project/REFLAXE_INTEGRATION_FORK_POLICY.md. Start with direct semantic-envelope, root-replacement, and cache regressions. Keep existing non-opted-in targets behavior-compatible. The API must be useful to the Reflaxe compiler family and must not contain OCaml semantics, preserve arbitrary metadata blindly, expose host object identity, or become a universal IR/pass manager. Reconcile repeated onAfterTyping batches and isolate persistent caches by exact revisions. Sign the commit and PR body with the required hxhx-agent incident statement.
acceptance_criteria: 1) A preserve declaration that loses an envelope fails with the responsible preprocessor and family. 2) Declared invalidate plus target recomputation succeeds; invalidation without recomputation fails at the final validator. 3) Root replacement changes the body revision and cannot retain an old analysis. 4) Repeated onAfterTyping batches are reconciled rather than overwritten. 5) Server revisions cannot share mutable ClassFuncData or stale plans. 6) Existing non-opted-in target output remains unchanged. 7) Trace on/off is deterministic and output-inert. 8) The work occurs in a clean worktree, passes the Reflaxe suite and a compatibility target, and lands through a signed Reflaxe PR linked from haxe_ocaml-7201t.
close_reason: Target-neutral revisioned semantic lifecycle landed in fullofcaffeine/reflaxe PR #8 at merge commit f4f7948142a4d32614d45e9369c38bc50da1baa2 with local matrix, compiler-server regression, and six green fork CI checks; OCaml target integration is deliberately tracked separately.

title: Route expensive hxhx and real-compiler QA by risk
description: Keep hxhx as a strong downstream reflaxe.ocaml consumer and retain a real Reflaxe-compiler-to-plugin end-to-end proof without rebuilding or exercising the full compiler stack for every unrelated change. Make the cheap target lanes the normal feedback loop and reserve bounded hxhx canaries plus authentic compiler promotion for the changes and release phases that can invalidate those contracts.
design: Add one deterministic changed-surface and event classifier with a cheap always-run aggregate so required checks never hang merely because an expensive job was intentionally skipped. Q0/Q1 remain the normal reflaxe.ocaml compiler, runtime, example, and package lanes. Run bounded Q2 hxhx and plugin canaries for touched target/runtime/bootstrap/plugin contracts and candidate promotions. Run Q3 large hxhx self-compile/bootstrap plus the authentic promoted Reflaxe compiler on schedules, release candidates, manual requests, and explicitly classified high-risk changes. Q4 remains hxhx release evidence. Unknown relevant paths escalate safely. Reuse one immutable reflaxe.ocaml candidate and one built hxhx artifact across a matrix where possible, record runner time and cache/artifact identity, and never make hxhx the sole reflaxe.ocaml release authority.
acceptance_criteria: 1) Inventory current push/PR workflows, hxhx builds, trigger paths, recent durations, and the docs-only baseline. 2) A reviewed machine-checked map assigns changes and events to Q0-Q4, with safe escalation for unknown compiler/runtime/ABI paths and an explicit manual override. 3) Documentation-only and unrelated target changes complete a cheap required aggregate without building hxhx or running authentic promotion E2E. 4) Relevant reflaxe.ocaml target/runtime/bootstrap/plugin changes and release candidates trigger the bounded exact-artifact hxhx canary; scheduled/manual/release and classified high-risk events trigger the large consumer E2E. 5) One nontrivial Haxe-authored Reflaxe compiler remains a retained QA workload across evaluated, stock-Haxe plugin, hxhx plugin, and hxhx builtin forms; toy probes cannot substitute for its scheduled or release proof. 6) Jobs share immutable package, target-core, plugin payload, and hxhx build artifacts where safe and verify every digest before reuse. 7) Failure summaries identify producer SHA, artifact digest, consumer SHA, tier, trigger reason, ABI/toolchain identity, and runtime result. 8) Before/after workflow count, runner time, setup/build duplication, latency, and false-skip evidence are reported without weakening standalone target or hxhx release gates. 9) Exact pushed workflow checks, docs, README Goals, and North Star impact are reviewed before closure.

title: Own feature-gated typed bodies before OCaml semantic lowering
description: The exact installed reflaxe.ocaml package passes hosted Linux and a local arm64 Mac but fails on hosted macOS. Independent review and local source inspection now identify the direct defect: PreservePlaceAssignmentsImpl wraps an admitted update, Everything-Is-An-Expression preserves it, and the final Reflaxe RemovePureExpressions pass discards the target-owned metadata while retaining the update. The OCaml builder then correctly rejects the unowned operation. The host-specific trigger remains open; define one revisioned lifecycle in which early protection survives semantic rewrites and final plans describe the exact body emitted.
design: Use the accepted GPT-5.6 B+C+D boundary. First add a direct marker-loss regression, a full preprocessor-order regression, a minimal feature-gated fixture, and bounded output-inert tracing. Then introduce separate early protection and final revision-bound admission/planning, with no expression preprocessor after sealing. Add a narrow target-neutral Reflaxe contract for immutable function input, declared opaque-envelope effects, final validation, repeated onAfterTyping reconciliation, and revision-safe caches through a separate Reflaxe worktree and PR. Keep the builder mechanical and retain the fail-closed invariant. Do not hand-tag source, rewrite Exception until CI moves, disable DCE, preserve all metadata blindly, rebind in the builder, add raw/Dynamic fallback, or introduce a broad IR/CFG.
acceptance_criteria: 1) A direct unit and full-order test prove the current marker loss and then pass through a declared preserve/consume/rebuild lifecycle. 2) A focused @:ifFeature fixture reproduces the route independently of Exception.hx and bounded traces identify final retained bodies, origins, and revisions without changing output. 3) Every emitted admitted operation has early protection before semantic rewrites and one immutable plan for the exact sealed body revision. 4) Repeated onAfterTyping batches and compiler-server revisions cannot reuse incomplete or stale mutable ClassFuncData. 5) The narrow Reflaxe contract lands through its own signed worktree/PR and existing non-opted-in targets remain unchanged. 6) Hosted Linux, hosted arm64 macOS, and local arm64 macOS pass the same verified package under exact toolchain/framework provenance. 7) No source hand-tags, DCE weakening, target-stdlib whack-a-mole, builder rebinding, legacy fallback, raw OCaml, Dynamic, or broad IR/CFG is introduced. 8) Review provenance, formatting, architecture, package evidence, README Goals, and North Star impact are recorded before closure.
close_reason: Feature-gated typed bodies now retain target ownership through a revisioned Reflaxe lifecycle and one sealed OCaml place-plan path; exact local and hosted Linux/macOS package evidence passes with immutable framework provenance and no fallback.

title: Own a complete generated OCaml artifact manifest
description: Make every compiler-owned source, project file, report, and package input in a reflaxe.ocaml output explicit before offering reproducible source bundles. The current Reflaxe _GeneratedFiles.json receipt covers emitted Haxe modules only; it omits target-owned files added afterward, so it is not a safe packaging manifest.
design: Introduce one deterministic target-owned artifact manifest assembled at the point each producer writes an output. Record safe relative path, artifact kind, owner, source/generated status, digest, profile eligibility, and the program/configuration revision. Cover Reflaxe modules, the type registry, entry modules, Dune files, runtime sources, reports, aliases, inferred interfaces, generated bindings/adapters, and curated export wrappers as those producers exist. Consume typed runtime and native dependency/source manifests rather than scanning output directories or generated Dune text. Build/install/bundle tooling must fail on missing, duplicate, stale, modified, or unattributed artifacts.
acceptance_criteria: 1) Every compiler-owned non-cache file in representative executable, library, plugin, selective-runtime, and report-enabled outputs is present exactly once with a stable owner and SHA-256 digest. 2) The manifest is deterministic for the same normalized program/configuration and rejects unsafe paths, duplicates, missing files, digest mismatches, unknown owners, and stale revisions. 3) Runtime entries agree with the locked semantic runtime manifest, and external/native sources agree with the structured dependency/source manifest; no directory sweep or Dune/source text inference is authoritative. 4) inspect presents the manifest without overstating release readiness. 5) a clean source bundle can be built solely from the checked manifest plus its dependency lock, rebuilt in a clean environment, and compared with the original manifest. 6) negative fixtures prove an unrecorded target file and an extra output-directory file cannot silently enter a package. 7) provenance/license ownership and README/North Star impact are explicitly reviewed.

comments.author: Marcelo Serpa
comments.text: XHIGH IMPLEMENTATION BOUNDARY — The existing GPT-5.6 native-power review supplies the independent architecture pass; this local second pass narrows it to current output ownership. A fresh place-assignment build proved that _GeneratedFiles.json names only Haxe-emitted module files while 43 current target-owned files are absent, including the type registry, package aliases, Dune project/entry files, runtime sources, and compiler reports. The first hard-cut slice will introduce one request-local target registry. Each producer records a safe output-relative path and plain-language ownership facts when it writes the file; a final filesystem walk may only reject an unregistered non-cache file and may never infer its owner from a filename or generated Dune/source text. Previous manifest entries may be removed only when their recorded digest still matches, so cleanup cannot erase a user-modified file.\n\nThe manifest will distinguish reproducible source-bundle inputs from volatile measurement evidence. Every recorded file still receives its real SHA-256 digest, but elapsed-time reports do not affect the stable source-bundle revision. _GeneratedFiles.json remains framework bookkeeping and is imported as the module inventory rather than packaged as target source. The current syntax-derived runtime selection and free-form native libraries will be labeled incomplete authorities; source bundling must remain unavailable until haxe_ocaml-0uwin and haxe_ocaml-v8a9b provide the reviewed semantic runtime and dependency locks. Inspect may report the manifest as internally valid, but it must not call the output release-ready. This slice adds no readiness-bar change and no broad output-directory packaging sweep.

comments.text: CHECKPOINT — Added the output-inert artifact-manifest model, schema validator, and transaction builder as three focused modules. The model uses closed producer/file/source vocabularies, stable program and configuration revisions, per-file SHA-256/byte counts, separate stable source-bundle and full artifact-set revisions, and explicit incomplete runtime/dependency authorities. The builder rejects unsafe paths, duplicate or unknown claims, missing files, unattributed output files, stale manifest revisions, and changed obsolete files; it removes a previous compiler-owned file only when its recorded digest still matches. Volatile timing evidence is inventoried but cannot change the reproducible source-bundle revision. A new fast null-safe Haxe fixture covers positive and negative cases and is included in ci:guards. This checkpoint does not change generated output yet, does not enable bundling, and does not change README/North Star readiness bars. Verified with npm run test:reflaxe-ocaml:artifact-manifest, npm run guard:hx-format:changed, npm run guard:mega-file-gravity-watch, and git diff --check.

comments.author: Marcelo Serpa
comments.text: INTEGRATION CHECKPOINT — The manifest now covers current executable, library, plugin, selective-runtime, inferred-interface, lowering-report, lifecycle-trace, and build-timing outputs. `inspect` rechecks every recorded digest and reports generated-file ownership separately from source-bundle readiness. Runtime selection and native dependencies remain explicit blockers, so this does not enable packaging or change README/North Star readiness bars. During repeat-build testing, inferred `.mli` files alternated between present and absent. The cause was a relative output path stored by the manifest while Dune temporarily changed the process working directory; the next build looked under `output/output`, failed to recognize the prior compiler-owned interfaces, and removed them as obsolete. The builder now anchors the output directory once as an absolute path. A fast working-directory regression and the real two-build `ocaml_mli` integration test both prove the fix. title: Publish the neutral MIT Haxe-family heavy-run package
description: The package review proved that hxhx plus three peer adapters share one stable protocol core, but another local copy is now prohibited. Prove clean npm install, cached offline npm install, Yarn 1 install, missing-package and tamper failures, local fixture behavior, two-way interoperability with a still-local v1 adapter, and one-consumer-at-a-time hard cutover. Unknown schema versions stay fail-closed; rollback pins the previous exact version and never auto-deletes an unknown lease.
acceptance_criteria: 1) A human-approved neutral public repository, package name, maintainers, signing/release authority, and MIT provenance record exist. 2) The dependency-free CommonJS API/CLI passes Node 20 and Node 22 matrices and produces immutable provenance-backed artifacts. 3) Exact lockfile-pinned npm and Yarn consumers pass clean, cached-offline, missing-package, and tamper tests. 4) Two-way v1 interoperability passes before hard-cutting one current adapter; no dual production implementation remains. 5) Schema upgrade and rollback procedures are executable and fail closed. 6) README Goals/North Star readiness is reviewed without inflation.

comments.author: Marcelo Serpa
comments.text: Explicit thinking:xhigh second-pass review: (1) publishing from the current private haxe.ocaml root is rejected because consumers could not independently audit or fetch its release history; (2) making a GPL target repository the owner is rejected because protocol maintenance is cross-target and future MIT provenance would become ambiguous; (3) a relative workspace, private Git SHA, vendored unpublished tarball, or moving checkout is less reproducible and worsens offline failure behavior; (4) a fourth peer core copy is rejected because the three current peer cores are already byte-identical and the next repair would require coordinated edits. A neutral public MIT owner with exact immutable artifacts is therefore the only acceptable extraction seam. Architecture and tests are bounded; implementation is blocked only on human authority for the public repository/package namespace, maintainers, and publishing credentials. No Oracle is needed yet because the technical seam is clear; use it only if provenance, signing, or schema-version policy becomes ambiguous after those product choices.

title: Preserve stable typed-place origins in hxhx self-build
description: The full hxhx target end-to-end lane now reaches a compiler-authored instance-field update in NekoMacroExprLowering.hx that the typed OCaml place planner admits but cannot assign a stable structural origin. comments.text:
CLOSURE EVIDENCE — 2026-07-21

Practical outcome: a developer can ask a heavyweight local compiler check to wait for a bounded time instead of repeatedly retrying it or starting another expensive process on an already busy machine. The attached command reports only meaningful changes in why it is waiting, starts only after the existing capacity policy admits it, and records how long admission took. Commit 41fe774f4 introduced the shared haxe-family.heavy-run-lease.v1 protocol in hxhx. A lease is a small user-scoped ownership record that lets participating repositories take turns running their expensive local suites. It identifies the owning process safely, renews while that process is alive, recovers abandoned or reused-process records, supports a nested check without releasing its parent owner's lease, and never signals or kills another process. Success, failure, cancellation, and signals release only a lease owned by the current run.

The cross-repository requirement is now production evidence rather than only a proposal. Reflaxe.Ruby pull request 21 merged as bb2c9263ce55f892b621cad7ec46701f3268e641 on 2026-07-20. The executable compatibility fixture already proved Ruby blocking hxhx, hxhx blocking Ruby, and nested Ruby work leaving the outer hxhx lease intact. Therefore at least two independent repositories now coordinate through the same protocol.

Deterministic and live fixtures cover immediate admission, delayed admission, changed blocking reasons without polling spam, timeout, cancellation, active competition, nonparticipating external load, malformed/schema-mismatched state, dead and reused owners, heartbeat, nested handoff, and success/failure/signal cleanup. title: Plan mutable OCaml static storage before type emission
description: Same-module cross-type static assignment can currently generate an initializer that writes a ref cell before that cell is declared. The existing requestForwardMutableStatic mechanism is discovered while emitting a later function body, which is too late when the owning type fragment was already generated. Introduce a program or module-level static storage plan before type emission so mutable cells and their initialization order are sound and reusable by typed place lowering.
design: Inventory static declaration, initialization, read, write, compound-update, and module-fragment ordering. Build one immutable module-level plan from the typed program before any class fragment is printed. Declare required mutable ref cells before every initializer or function that can reference them, then emit initialization in Haxe-observable order. Keep semantic type separate from the OCaml carrier, preserve cross-module dependency order, and make both the typed place path and remaining legacy consumers read the same plan during migration. Do not patch generated OCaml text or add another late request side channel.
acceptance_criteria: 1) A focused same-Haxe-module, cross-type fixture compiles regardless of type traversal order. 2) Every mutable static cell is declared exactly once before reads, writes, and initializer assignments. 3) Static initialization order and side effects match upstream Haxe 4.3.7 for focused same-module, cross-module, dependency-cycle, and failure cases. 4) The plan records stable owner/symbol/type/carrier/init identities and deterministic order before target syntax. 5) Simple assignment, compound assignment, and updates can consume the plan without late declaration requests. 6) Missing, duplicate, cyclic, or representation-incompatible facts fail before OCaml compilation. 7) Generated-shape, native behavior, determinism, bootstrap snapshot, portable corpus, mega-file, and current-source guards pass. 8) README/North Star readiness and deferred place scope are reviewed honestly.

comments.author: Marcelo Serpa
comments.text: Discovery evidence from the typed static-assignment slice: a secondary SameModuleHolder type declared in Main.hx produced a write to samemoduleholder_value before that ref cell had been emitted, and native OCaml compilation failed with an unbound-value error. The current requestForwardMutableStatic side channel is populated only while the later Main method body is being built, so it cannot reliably affect a type fragment already emitted. The admitted typed slice now excludes same-module cross-type statics and has no late declaration side effect. The fix must inventory and order mutable static storage before any type syntax is emitted, then make both legacy reads/writes and typed places consume that immutable plan.

title: Centralize exhaustive OCaml target-AST traversal
description: Make every child of the OCaml target syntax tree visible through one authoritative traversal contract. Today the printer, runtime scanner, identifier analyses, and compiler helpers each switch over OcamlExpr independently, so a new child-bearing constructor can compile while one consumer silently misses it. This work is infrastructure for reliable syntax validation and runtime consistency checks; it does not replace the typed OCaml lowering model or introduce a broad pass manager.
design: 1. Inventory every OcamlExpr constructor and independent recursive consumer. 2. Add one exhaustive immediate-child mapping/folding schema with no catch-all leaf case, including children inside match cases, labelled arguments, records, annotations, and position wrappers. 3. Add constructor-coverage and sentinel-child tests so a new constructor fails until traversal policy is declared. 4. Introduce deterministic walk/fold helpers and explicit raw-node policy. 5. Migrate generic analyses one at a time while preserving generated bytes and behavior; keep scope-aware or printer-specific logic separate where semantics differ. 6. Do not mix this infrastructure slice with place lowering, pass reordering, runtime ABI changes, or printer rewrites.
acceptance_criteria: 1) One documented exhaustive immediate-child schema covers every OcamlExpr constructor and nested child container. 2) CI fails when a constructor is added without traversal coverage. 3) Identity mapping preserves every constructor structurally, and walk/fold child inventories agree under the same policy. 4) Raw nodes and source-position wrappers have explicit traversal semantics. 5) Runtime usage collection and duplicated identifier scans migrate through reviewable output-inert slices or document why a scope-aware variant is required. 6) Generated output, focused runtime selection, formatting, determinism, and the complete portable corpus remain green. 7) README Goals and North Star readiness are reviewed without inflating progress for infrastructure alone.
notes: Created from the modern Reflaxe architecture template review. This adopts its exhaustive traversal and constructor-coverage discipline while retaining the accepted GPT-5.6 C-lite OCaml lowering architecture populated through vertical slices.
close_reason: The OCaml target AST now has one exhaustive structural child contract with constructor and sentinel coverage, deterministic map/walk/fold behavior, explicit raw/position policy, and RuntimeUsageCollector migrated to it. Focused tests, complete portable conformance, full official formatting, guards, artifact hygiene, and a manual second pass are green; scope-aware identifier semantics are correctly separated into haxe_ocaml-i9bnd.1.

comments.author: Marcelo Serpa
comments.text:

It covers labelled arguments, match/try patterns and guards, record fields, annotations, and EPos; ERaw is an explicitly opaque leaf. Identity mapping preserves original nodes and arrays, and deterministic walk/fold are derived from the same schema. RuntimeUsageCollector is the first output-inert consumer migration. The existing printer test entrypoint now exercises constructor-set coverage, sentinel children, identity structure, walk/fold order, and structured runtime discovery; focused printer and M6 runtime-selection tests pass.

Three identifier consumers deliberately remain outside the blind structural walker: OcamlCompiler's parameter-use probe is a syntactic mention query, OcamlBuilder's parameter-use probe has lexical-shadowing policy, and OcamlCompiler.collectFreeIdents owns recursive-binding dependency analysis. Collapsing them into a plain walk would change binding meaning. A later output-inert slice should introduce one explicit scope-aware identifier contract and differential-test shadowing before replacing them. The shared traversal module documents this boundary now.

README Goals/North Star bars remain unchanged: this is reliability infrastructure and does not add user-visible target support. Full portable and broad guards remain pending until the currently overloaded machine has a credible capacity window.
